items.title: Trouver.tn met en relation particuliers et professionnels
items.description: Trouver.tn met en relation des particuliers qui cherchent un professionnel (produit ou service) avec des professionnels partout en Tunisie, sur le principe : vous décrivez votre besoin, les professionnels intéressés vous contactent. Lancé fin septembre 2026 par Hamza Chelligue, le site Trouver.tn propose des annonces de ventes de produits divers, des offres de formation et des offres d’emploi en Tunisie. Il compte déjà plus de 250 inscrits, dont 78 professionnels, et près de 200 demandes et offres publiées en un mois. Le principe est simple : au lieu de chercher un plombier, un plâtrier, un professeur ou un fournisseur, le particulier publie gratuitement sa demande, et les professionnels de sa délégation lui répondent. Le particulier choisit ensuite qui peut le contacter. Le site couvre les 24 gouvernorats et leurs 279 délégations. Il fonctionne en français et en darija, et une version anglaise vient d’ouvrir pour les Tunisiens de l’étranger qui ont besoin d’un service au pays. Publier une demande en tant que particulier et y répondre en tant que professionnel sont entièrement gratuits, sans limite. Seule la description de la demande est publique. Les coordonnées ne sont révélées qu’aux professionnels que l’on approuve individuellement, un par un. L’article Trouver.tn met en relation particuliers et professionnels est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Africa’s next great traveller is already at the departure gate
items.description: For decades, Africa’s tourism industry has been preoccupied with bringing the world to its shores. A landmark Skift study commissioned by Millat Group suggests that the continent’s next great tourism opportunity may lie in the opposite direction: the African traveller going out. For as long as the African tourism industry has been discussing its prospects, the conversation has largely revolved around one question: how do we get more international visitors to come to Africa? How do we persuade more Europeans to experience our beaches, more Americans to explore our wildlife and heritage, and more Asians to discover the continent’s extraordinary cultural and natural attractions? It is an understandable preoccupation. Africa accounts for approximately 19% of the world’s population but attracts only about 5% of international tourist arrivals. The continent has long been viewed as a destination waiting to be discovered, marketed and developed. But what if the industry’s next great opportunity is not necessarily about who is coming to Africa, but who is leaving it? That is the provocative proposition advanced by Africa in Motion: The Next Great Traveller , a new white paper produced by global travel intelligence company Skift and commissioned by Millat Group. Unveiled around World Travel Market London, the study attempts to quantify a market that has received remarkably little attention in the global tourism conversation: Africa’s outbound traveller. Its findings suggest that a significant shift is already under way, one that could reshape the continent’s relationship with global tourism over the next two decades. Across five focus markets – Egypt, Ethiopia, Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa – outbound international trips are projected to increase from 13.3 million in 2025 to 19.4 million by 2035. More immediately, outbound travel expenditure across these markets is forecast to rise from US$18.9 billion in 2025 to US$30.4 billion by 2030, representing growth of approximately 61%. These are not insignificant numbers. They point to the emergence of a new generation of African consumers whose aspirations, incomes, family connections and business interests increasingly extend beyond national and continental borders. As Hamza Farooqui, founder and chief executive of Millat Group, observes, the traditional emphasis on bringing tourists to Africa tells only half the story. The African traveller going out deserves equal attention. The Value Is Not Always in The Volume Perhaps the most revealing finding in the research is the distinction between the number of people travelling and the money they spend. Nigeria provides the clearest illustration. It ranks seventh among the eight African markets examined for outbound departures but first in total outbound expenditure, recording an estimated US$7.7 billion in 2025. That is approximately 41% more than South Africa, despite South Africa generating roughly five times as many outbound trips. The explanation lies in the profile of the Nigerian traveller. Demand is concentrated among relatively affluent consumers in Lagos and Abuja, with international travel driven substantially by business, high-end leisure and connections with family and friends abroad. The report estimates that diaspora-connected travel accounts for between 22% and 26% of outbound trips across the markets studied but generates between 40% 45% of expenditure. This segment is inferred from travel patterns and remittance corridors rather than directly measured through a dedicated survey, but its commercial significance is considerable. These are travellers visiting relatives, attending weddings and funerals, participating in family events and fulfilling educational and business commitments. Their journeys often last two to four weeks and are less dependent on promotional airfares than conventional leisure travel. For Ghana, this should be an especially interesting finding.The study identifies Ghana, alongside Nigeria and Zimbabwe, as a leading market for its Diaspora Connector segment. The Lagos-Accra corridor is also among the continent’s busiest intra-African air routes. Ghana’s connections with its diaspora in the United Kingdom, United States, Europe and elsewhere provide an established foundation for this market. December travel, family reunions, festivals, weddings and heritage visits are already familiar features of the country’s tourism calendar. The opportunity is to move beyond treating these journeys as occasional seasonal traffic and develop products and services around a year-round market. Airlines, hotels, travel management companies, tour operators and destination businesses could all benefit from understanding the needs of this traveller more deliberately. Africa Is Also Its Own Tourism Market There is another important dimension to the report: the movement of Africans within Africa. Approximately 40% of international arrivals on the continent are generated by travellers from other African countries. At several destinations examined in the study, regional visitors account for more than half of international arrivals. This is an important reminder that African tourism is not sustained exclusively by visitors arriving from distant markets. Regional travellers provide a significant occupancy base for hotels, support restaurants and entertainment businesses, and sustain demand across the continent’s travel ecosystem. The problem is that the infrastructure to serve this market remains inadequate. Only around 19% of intra-African routes have direct flights, while just seven of Africa’s 54 countries offer direct air connections to more than 20 other African nations. The consequences are familiar to anyone who has attempted to travel between neighbouring African countries. Journeys that should be relatively straightforward can involve connections through European or Middle Eastern hubs, adding time and cost. The Abidjan-Lagos coastal corridor alone carries an estimated 47 million people annually, much of that movement taking place by road. The Single African Air Transport Market offers a potential solution. Full implementation is modelled to increase GDP by US$4.2 billion, create approximately 600,000 jobs and reduce airfares by 27%. But political commitments must translate into actual route liberalisation, greater competition and more affordable air travel. There is little value in promoting regional tourism while maintaining policies that make it difficult for Africans to visit neighbouring countries. Hamza Farooqui, CEO, The Millat Group says these imbalances require a coordinated response from governments, airlines, hotel operators and investors. “We cannot keep talking about Africa’s tourism potential while making it difficult and expensive for Africans to travel across their own continent. “We need better connections between our cities, more accessible capital and accommodation that reflects how people actually travel. And we need to develop African businesses and operating expertise, not simply rely on international brands to deliver that growth.” The Gulf Is Already Positioning Itself One of the more fascinating aspects of the study is its examination of the growing relationship between African travellers and the Gulf. Dubai, Doha and Abu Dhabi have become much more than destinations. They are increasingly important interchange points connecting African passengers to Europe, Asia and North America. Approximately 28% of South Africa’s connecting traffic to Europe passes through Gulf hubs. The report also identifies substantial air capacity linking Johannesburg, Addis Ababa and Nairobi with major Gulf cities. The Gulf’s advantage is not simply its airlines or airports. It is also its willingness to make itself accessible. Visa policies, connectivity, hospitality infrastructure, cultural considerations and the development of products suited to African travellers have all contributed to its growing appeal. Türkiye provides another useful example. Its visa arrangements for certain African nationalities, combined with cultural and hospitality offerings, have helped it become a more attractive destination than traditional Western markets for some African travellers. The lesson is straightforward: destinations that make travelling easier stand to benefit from demand that might otherwise go elsewhere. Building For the Traveller of Tomorrow The implications extend beyond aviation and destination marketing to the hospitality investment landscape. Africa currently has 123,846 branded hotel rooms in its development pipeline, spread across 675 properties. Yet the report identifies a striking mismatch between the accommodation being developed and the market expected to drive much of the continent’s growth. Only 14 of the 168 hotel brands with signed development deals are positioned in the economy or midscale categories. Meanwhile, the study identifies the US$150 to US$400-a-night segment as an underserved opportunity. This is particularly relevant to younger, urban, aspirational and regionally mobile travellers who want quality, convenience and distinctive experiences without necessarily paying luxury hotel rates. There is a danger that the industry could continue investing heavily in the top end of the market while overlooking the much larger opportunity developing in the middle. For investors, this is an important distinction. The next phase of African tourism growth will require not just more hotel rooms, but the right rooms in the right locations at prices that match the emerging consumer. A Different Tourism Conversation There are, of course, significant obstacles. African passengers departing from the continent face some of the world’s highest aviation taxes and charges. The average international departure attracts approximately US$68 in taxes and charges, compared with US$32 in Europe. In West Africa, the average rises to US$109.50. Airline profitability is another constraint. African carriers generated an estimated US$0.90 profit per passenger in 2024, compared with US$15.20 for Middle Eastern carriers. Expanding connectivity will therefore require a more commercially sustainable aviation environment. For Ghana and the wider West African tourism industry, the message is particularly relevant. The region has a substantial diaspora market, strong cultural connections, significant business travel potential and considerable intra-African movement. Yet high travel costs and inadequate direct connectivity continue to limit its potential. The broader lesson from Africa in Motion is that tourism policy, marketing and investment must evolve alongside the traveller. For decades, the industry has organised itself around the ambition of moving the world into Africa. That ambition remains important. But a growing African population with increasing purchasing power, international connections and global aspirations is creating another market that cannot be ignored. The next generation of African travellers is not waiting to be discovered. They are already travelling, spending and making choices about where their money goes. The question is whether Africa’s airlines, hotels, investors and tourism authorities will recognise the opportunity quickly enough to build for them. As the report aptly concludes, the question is no longer whether these travellers exist. It is who builds for them first. Click here for the full report: https://millatglobal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Millat_Skift-White-Paper-Africa-in-Motion.pdf The Author: Francis Doku is the founder and CEO of Maestro Africa Group, Publisher and Managing Editor of Africa Meets Magazine, and Executive Producer and Host of the Africa Rising Podcast. He also serves as West Africa Regional Director of Africa Tourism Partners and is a Consulting Editor and contributor to VoyagesAfriq. Doku writes on tourism, culture, international relations and Africa’s evolving engagement with the world.

items.title: Four decades of biodiversity conservation: Goziir calls for greater support to sustain long-standing environmental efforts
items.description: For more than four decades, since 1980, the people of Goziir in the Nandom Municipality of the Upper West Region have demonstrated a remarkable commitment to environmental conservation by maintaining a strong community-wide culture of bushfire prevention and protecting local biodiversity. As a predominantly farming community, Goziir is located in the western corridor of the Nandom Municipality and is widely recognised for its environmental preservation efforts and intensive agricultural activities. The initiative, championed by the late Chief of Goziir, Naa Leo Aamwaa Yiryel II, and 10 other elders, has become an exemplary model of how traditional leadership, community participation, local rules and collective responsibility can contribute to sustainable land management and environmental protection. One of the primary reasons behind the initiative was to prevent livestock, particularly cattle, from migrating long distances in search of pasture, sometimes failing to return to the community or falling prey to theft by unidentified persons. The late chief and his elders therefore introduced a no-bushfire system to ensure year-round pasture for livestock, encouraging the animals to remain within the community. The community’s experience offers valuable lessons for other areas in the Nandom Municipality, the Upper West Region and Ghana as a whole, particularly as bushfires continue to threaten vegetation, soil fertility, agricultural production, livestock and biodiversity. During a visit to Goziir, I engaged the community’s traditional leader, an agriculture officer, residents, the assembly member, the Municipal Chief Executive (MCE) and the Upper West Regional Director of the Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) to explore the achievements of the conservation initiative, the challenges involved in sustaining it and the support required to encourage other communities to adopt similar practices. Although the initiative is rooted in local traditions, its benefits extend beyond Goziir, demonstrating the potential of community-led conservation to strengthen climate resilience, promote sustainable agriculture and protect natural resources. Traditional leadership and community ownership The current Chief of Goziir, Naa Aamwaa Simon Yiryel III, identified community participation, traditional sanctions and collective responsibility as key factors behind the community’s long-standing success in preventing bushfires. Speaking during the visit, Naa Yiryel explained that the community had developed and enforced its own rules against bush burning rather than relying solely on bylaws enacted by the Nandom Municipal Assembly. Under these traditional arrangements, anyone found deliberately setting fire to the bush is summoned before the chief and his elders. He recalled that, in the past, offenders were required to carry large stones from the hills and pile them up as a deterrent to others. The chief stressed that the success of the initiative depended not simply on imposing rules but also on ensuring that residents understood the harmful effects of bushfires and the collective benefits of protecting the environment. “The people must understand why we have to protect our environment. When they understand the benefits, they are more willing to support the initiative,” Naa Aamwaa Simon Yiryel III emphasised. He noted that residents who understood the importance of conservation were more responsive when called upon to help prevent or control fires, including through signals sounded at night. The initiative has also contributed to improved livestock management, better agricultural yields and stronger social cohesion. Preventing bushfires helps keep cattle within the community rather than allowing them to wander in search of pasture. Meanwhile, decomposing grass adds organic matter to the soil, improving its fertility and reducing farmers’ dependence on expensive chemical fertilisers. Beyond these economic benefits, the shared commitment has strengthened community unity. The no-bushfire rule covers the entire community, alongside an additional protected forest area where tree felling and bush burning are strictly prohibited. Agricultural perspectives and replication An agriculture officer at the Nandom Municipal Assembly, Gaeten Bomansaan Baligi, has called for the replication of Goziir’s zero-bushfire model in other communities to strengthen environmental protection and climate resilience. Mr Baligi said the Department of Agriculture could support such efforts through farmer education and capacity-building programmes in climate-smart and conservation agriculture. He also suggested organising study tours to Goziir to enable farmers from other communities to observe its sustainable farming practices firsthand. While noting that Goziir had demonstrated that farming could thrive without routine bush burning, he expressed concern about post-harvest bush burning in other parts of the municipality and stressed the need for intensified public education to change attitudes. Lessons on discipline and sustainability The Upper West Regional Director of the Environmental Protection Authority (EPA), Mr Jonas Kpierekoh, drawing on his knowledge of Goziir’s conservation model, cautioned that although the initiative had national potential, weak leadership, favouritism, jealousy and greed could undermine similar efforts elsewhere. Drawing on accounts dating back to around 1955, Mr Kpierekoh emphasised that sustainable conservation required disciplined leadership, as demonstrated by Goziir, and the fair enforcement of rules, irrespective of an offender’s social connections or family background. He also warned that jealousy and the desire for personal recognition could create conflicts, citing instances in other communities where conservation initiatives had been undermined because individuals prioritised personal recognition over collective benefits. Despite these challenges, he noted that Goziir’s protected areas also served as important sources of traditional medicinal herbs. Staneslos Nasaal, a former Agriculture Officer for Nandom, highlighted the importance of public education, community mobilisation and volunteer fire teams in sustaining conservation efforts. He explained that changing attitudes required patience and continuous engagement, noting that early adopters, such as those behind Goziir’s initiative, played a crucial role in influencing others by demonstrating the benefits of conservation. He also highlighted the success of training volunteer fire groups in collaboration with the Ghana National Fire Service. Local government support and future outlook The Assembly Member for the Goziir Electoral Area, Sebastian Gan, has appealed to the Nandom Municipal Assembly and relevant government agencies to provide greater support for the community’s conservation efforts and help formalise its local rules. Mr Gan said maintaining a bushfire-free environment required constant vigilance, particularly among the youth. He recalled a late-night mobilisation on December 31 to combat a bushfire with support from the Ghana National Fire Service. He urged the authorities to provide tangible development support to recognise the community’s decades of commitment to environmental protection. In response, the Municipal Chief Executive for Nandom, Anthony Ziniyel, said the Assembly was exploring possible incentives, including annual awards and development projects, to encourage other communities to emulate Goziir’s example. Although the Assembly does not have a dedicated fund for the initiative, the MCE indicated that a community’s environmental record could be considered when allocating development projects, such as school blocks and other infrastructure through the Assembly Common Fund. He, however, clarified that the proposed incentives were still under consideration and would be subject to the Assembly’s standard planning and budgetary processes. On the issue of discipline and sanctions against offenders, Mr Ziniyel recounted an incident in which he and his elder brother were falsely accused of setting fire to a section of the bush in Goziir. “In fact, I recounted this day with pain. Because I was in the company of my elder brother, travelling along the road, and we realised that a portion of the bush was burning. Right there, some unidentified people quickly ran to the Goziir chief’s palace and lodged a complaint against my brother and me. To the surprise of both of us, we were severely punished and made to carry stones, blocks, among others. After the punishment, my brother ran down south and is currently based there. He only visits occasionally,” the MCE lamented. The Goziir experience underscores how community ownership, traditional leadership, public education, fair enforcement of local rules and collective action can drive long-term environmental conservation. As Ghana continues to pursue climate resilience and sustainable agriculture, Goziir stands as a shining example in the sub-region of how grassroots initiatives can complement broader national environmental goals. However, sustaining and expanding the model will require stronger institutional support, deliberate investment, public education and incentives to encourage other communities to embrace similar conservation practices.

items.title: Australia’s oldest department store David Jones folds after 188 years
items.description: David Jones, Australia’s oldest department store chain, has gone into voluntary administration, putting thousands of jobs at risk. It comes after years of financial struggles for the 188-year-old retailer – known locally as DJs – as customers desert traditional shops for online shopping. David Jones’s physical and online stores will continue to operate while receivers FTI Consulting review the company, said voluntary administrators McGrathNicol. “David Jones is an iconic company and so many Australians have stories and memories of visiting DJ’s stores,” said its CEO Erica Berthold, adding the brand has a “well-developed plan” to “reset the business for the future”. Berthold thanked “customers, our team members and our partners for their continued support of David Jones through this period”. David Jones employs about 6,000 staff and has 38 physical stores, with 17 of those in Westfield shopping centres. Hours before the board voted to go into administration, Scentre – which owns Westfield – said the retailer had not paid its rent for October and was “therefore in breach” of its tenancy agreement. “We understand the current retail trading environment, rising costs, a significant and outdated retail footprint, and supply chain challenges have led to this point,” said Christopher Hill from receivers FTI Consulting. By appointing administrators and receivers, David Jones will get “breathing space” and a chance to restructure the business, Hill said. For many Australians, David Jones – and its trademark black-and-white houndstooth design – represented luxury. But its collapse signalled the “death knell” for the department store format, said Jana Bowden, who teaches marketing at Macquarie University’s Business School. “It was once the epitome of glamour shopping in Australia – the Aussie version of Harrods,” she said, “a place you would go to see and be a part of the glitz and glamour, where you could marvel at all the premium luxury labels, and feel like you’d made it.” Visiting the flagship city stores in Sydney and Melbourne was also a ritual for many Australian families, especially to see the festive Christmas window displays. “People would travel from hours away from the city just to see those windows and experience the magic,” Bowden said, but in recent years, the brand had lost its shine. “The city stores have retained their upper end airs and graces, but the suburban stores leave a lot to be desired – they’re mundane, they lack excitement and there’s definitely no glitz,” she said. During Queen Elizabeth II’s first visit to Sydney in 1954, the then-27-year-old monarch attended a banquet dinner on the seventh floor of the Elizabeth St store, according to the Sydney Morning Herald.

items.title: FG allocates N2.1bn to revive OAUTHC renal programme — CMD
items.description: By Shina Abubakar, Osogbo The Federal Government has allocated N2.1 billion to the Obafemi Awolowo University Teaching Hospitals Complex (OAUTHC), Ile-Ife, Osun State, to revive its renal replacement programme, the hospital’s Chief Medical Director, Prof. John Okeniyi, has said. Okeniyi disclosed this on Thursday during the grand finale of the hospital’s 50th anniversary celebration at its complex in Ile-Ife. He said the planned revival of the programme was part of President Bola Tinubu’s Renewed Hope Agenda for the health sector. The CMD expressed optimism that the fund, when released and properly utilised, would restore the hospital’s renal replacement services and strengthen its capacity to provide kidney care for patients. “I would also like to thank President Bola Tinubu because we have up to N2.1 billion appropriated for our renal programme. By the time we do this and get the money, I believe the renal replacement programme will be fully back. That is part of the Renewed Hope Agenda,” he said. Meanwhile, a former Osun State Deputy Governor, Senator Iyiola Omisore, called for greater support for healthcare initiatives, stressing the importance of investing in interventions that improve people’s health and save lives. Omisore said healthcare was essential to human existence, urging individuals and stakeholders to support initiatives capable of making meaningful differences in people’s lives. “What I am trying to emphasise is that health is essential to life. That is why I consider this initiative important. I try to support causes that people will appreciate and that will make a meaningful difference in their lives. That is the reality of healthcare institutions and the importance of their services,” he said. Also speaking, Mr Seyi Tinubu, represented by the Chairman of the Tinubu/Shettima Grassroots Mobilisation, Lawal Umar, said healthcare achievements should be measured by their impact on ordinary Nigerians rather than policies and infrastructure alone. “Health achievement should not be judged by policies and buildings, but by whether ordinary Nigerians can access care, afford medicines and recover,” he said. The post FG allocates N2.1bn to revive OAUTHC renal programme — CMD appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Apapa Customs generates N302.9bn in October, warns against illicit trade
items.description: By Godwin Oritse The Apapa Area Command of the Nigeria Customs Service (NCS) generated N302.9 billion in revenue in October 2026, representing a 7.13 per cent increase over the N282.79 billion recorded in September 2026. In a statement issued by Isah Sulaiman, Chief Superintendent of Customs and Public Relations Officer of the Command, the October revenue performance reflects the Command’s sustained efforts to boost revenue generation while facilitating legitimate trade. The statement attributed the performance to the leadership of the Customs Area Controller (CAC), Comptroller Murtala Mu’azu, who assumed duty on September 29, 2026, with a commitment to stakeholder engagement, operational efficiency and improved service delivery. According to the statement, Comptroller Mu’azu has prioritised the Customs Service’s policy thrust of Consolidation, Collaboration and Innovation, with particular emphasis on addressing operational challenges confronting port users. This approach was reflected in a stakeholder engagement meeting held last month, which brought together importers, exporters, licensed customs agents, shipping companies and terminal operators to address issues including delays in Demand Notices, cargo clearance bottlenecks and other operational challenges. Beyond the meeting, the CAC has embarked on courtesy visits to key stakeholders and strategic partners within the port community to strengthen institutional relationship, promote mutual understanding and foster the collaboration needed to create a more conducive business environment for traders and other port users. As part of efforts to improve operational efficiency, the Command has also intensified the review and streamlining of Transire processing to eliminate unnecessary bureaucratic bottlenecks, improve inter-departmental coordination and reduce processing time without compromising compliance and control measures. items.title: The Democrats' historic duty
items.description: Thirty years. Eighty years, and even 90. Some of the positions Democratic candidates won in Tuesday’s midterm elections , from Senate seats to attorneys-general, have not had a blue occupant in decades. The outcome of this election, even more than the 2018 midterms, could reshape American politics and policy for years to come. But if the Democrats are to make the most of their gains, they must be ambitious—even audacious. The coming weeks will bring countless hot takes, deep dives, and data analyses. How did Democrats do it? What was the secret to their success in states like Kansas, South Carolina, and Texas? Which traditionally “red” voter cohorts turned “blue”? But the midterm results, like much of US politics over the last decade, come down to one constant: Donald Trump. Trump is the alpha and the omega of the MAGA era. Responsibility for the affordability crisis Americans are facing—a top priority driving the recent vote—falls squarely on his shoulders. His chaotic trade wars have driven up costs for big companies, small businesses, and ordinary consumers across the country, with the price of most products rising by about 3 per cent as a result of his tariffs. His war of choice in Iran —from the 2025 bombing of the country’s nuclear facilities to the large-scale attacks that have fueled geopolitical turmoil and halted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz since February 2026—drove up prices further, especially for fertilizer and diesel fuel. The result has been to alienate a core Trump constituency: white rural voters. It does not help that Trump has shown utter disregard for the people who are struggling due to his actions, instead bragging about the oil and gas industry making a “frickin’ fortune.” With his behavior becoming increasingly erratic, a significant segment of his supporters have had enough. Many stayed home on Tuesday, while some cast votes for Democrats. Independent voters, for their part, overwhelmingly backed the Democrats. But far from blindly celebrating this outcome, the incoming majority should view it as a cautionary tale. These swing voters are now negatively polarized: they vote for the party with which they are the least upset. They could easily turn against the Democrats in 2028 if they are not convinced to stick around. While anger at Trump was the main variable shaping the election’s outcome, the Democrats benefited from the high quality of their candidates in most key races. In states like Kansas, Pennsylvania, and Texas, candidates matched the local spirit with the anger of an overwhelmed electorate. Here, again, the Democrats are at risk of learning the wrong lesson: when the party’s moderate wing claims credit for flipping red states, it overlooks that the US remains in an anti-establishment, populist economic era. Many of the Democratic winners, such as Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, are self-described populists. Speaking to the New York Times before the election, Hinojosa observed that focusing on cultural issues was a trap and not what voters were looking for in 2026. She then ran a campaign that focused on Texans’ economic concerns, ousting Greg Abbott, who had spent the last 12 years concentrating political and administrative authority in his own hands, pandering to wealthy and corporate donors, and rigging the state’s congressional-district maps in Republicans’ favor. Populism, especially economic populism, gives professional Democrats hay fever. They find it aesthetically off-putting and incompatible with the dying neoliberal economic order to which they remain stubbornly devoted. But they will have to get over it. The time has come for the Democratic Party to cast aside institutional caution and broaden its ambition. AI is a good starting point. Contrary to the narrative that tech firms and their army of consultants have been pushing, American voters do, in fact, hate data centers . They also understand that unfettered AI development poses economic, social, and existential risks. If Congressional Democrats bow to Big Tech, they will soon find themselves back where they were two years ago. At the state level, new Democratic governors must understand the nature of their own power. To wait for a divided Washington to get things done while Trump still occupies the White House is to waste time. They should hit the ground running with bold, creative agendas that focus not just on bringing costs down, but also on pushing wages up. The affordability crisis is actually a money crisis. Over the next 18 months, the field for new ideas, systemic and economic, in the US will be the most open it is likely to be for decades. US voters have dealt Trump a sharp rebuke, which Democrats—indeed, all Americans—should celebrate. But the Democratic Party’s elation will need to cool and harden into determination. Where we are today is not where we need to be, nor is it where Americans expect to find themselves tomorrow, next year, or five years from now. This article was originally published on Project Syndicate and has been reproduced here with permission.

items.title: James Barnor named recipient of Sony World Photography Awards 2027 honour
items.description: Ghanaian photographer James Barnor has been named recipient of the Outstanding Contribution to Photography award at the 2027 Sony World Photography Awards. The announcement marks the 20th edition of the awards, which celebrate photographers from around the world and recognise their contributions to the medium. Recognised as Ghana’s first photojournalist, Barnor documented the country’s journey to independence in 1957 and later established its first colour photography laboratory. His work bridges continents and cultures, capturing Black communities in Accra and London during decades of profound transformation. Barnor is best known for his remarkable portraits, taken from the 1950s to the 1970s, celebrating the beauty, style and glamour of Black social life. From his renowned Ever Young studio to the streets of downtown Accra and central London, he captured the identities of his subjects, creating a visual archive of their daily lives. A retrospective of more than 50 works by Barnor will go on display at London’s Somerset House in April 2027, as part of a special presentation at the flagship Sony World Photography Awards exhibition. Following his journey from Accra to London, his studies in colour photography and his return to Ghana, the retrospective will bring together photographic prints and ephemera from across his career, highlighting moments that defined his practice. Born in 1929, Barnor trained under his cousin, portrait photographer J. P. D. Dodoo. In 1950, he became the first staff photographer at Ghana’s newly launched Daily Graphic , giving voice and representation to Ghanaians during a period of rapid social change. As a photojournalist, he documented this historic period through the eyes of those who lived it, capturing everything from rallies and street parades to Kwame Nkrumah’s declaration of independence. In 1953, he opened the Ever Young studio in Accra’s Jamestown district, where he photographed shop assistants, students and traffic officers alongside judges and political figures, capturing a society in the act of defining itself. Barnor moved to the UK in 1959 to deepen his technical knowledge of photography. He studied at Medway College of Art in Kent before working as a colour printer at Colour Processing Laboratories, one of Britain’s leading colour laboratories. During this period, he also worked for Drum , the influential Black South African lifestyle magazine known for its anti-apartheid reporting. His portraits of Black models and celebrities appeared on its covers and in its fashion pages. These images became part of a broader visual language of the African continent and its diaspora, serving as vital reference points for readers and inspiring photographers and artists for decades. Following training with Agfa-Gevaert in Belgium and Germany, Barnor returned to Ghana about a decade later as the company’s technical representative. He established the country’s first colour processing laboratory, introducing colour photography to new audiences while continuing to work as a photographer and journalist. His work was instrumental in shaping Ghana’s photographic tradition and paving the way for aspiring photographers across the region. In the early 1990s, Barnor settled back in London, where he lives today. His work has since been the subject of numerous exhibitions and publications. These include a touring retrospective curated by Hans Ulrich Obrist, which was shown at the Serpentine in London in 2021, MASI Lugano in Switzerland in 2022, and the Detroit Institute of Arts in the United States in 2023. James Barnor: Stories, Pictures from the Archive (1947-1987) , curated by Matthieu Humery, opened at LUMA Arles in France in 2022. The exhibition was accompanied by the launch of the James Barnor Prize, dedicated to African photographers. In October 2023, James Barnor, Studio of Life opened at FOMU Antwerp in Belgium. Coinciding with the photographer’s 95th birthday, the James Barnor 95 festival was held in Accra and Tamale in May 2024, featuring a month-long programme. In 2025, his work featured in the exhibition Ideas of Africa: Portraiture and Political Imagination at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in the United States. In 2026, Barnor’s work was shown as part of Ibrahim Mahama’s exhibition Le Temps des Récoltes at the Fondation Cartier pour l’art contemporain in France. Commenting on receiving the award, Barnor said: ‘I am honoured to receive this award. I was lucky to be born and brought up in a family of photographers, and I took full advantage of it to absorb as much as I could. When I opened my studio in Accra, I never imagined that my work would take me so far: through Ghana’s independence, to London and back again. My camera became my companion, and I have never regretted it. Wherever I went, I tried to learn so that I could share what I had learned. Today, that matters more to me than ever. Up-and-coming photographers now have every chance to go even further, and I hope this exhibition will inspire them to stay curious, to tell their own stories, and to pass on what they know.’ The Outstanding Contribution to Photography award recognises individuals behind some of the most groundbreaking photographic work of recent times. Barnor joins a distinguished list of previous recipients, including Martin Parr (2017), Graciela Iturbide (2021), Edward Burtynsky (2022), Sebastião Salgado (2024), Susan Meiselas (2025) and Joel Meyerowitz (2026). Barnor will receive the award at the annual gala ceremony in London on 15 April 2027, during which the overall winners of the Sony World Photography Awards 2027 will also be announced. About James Barnor Born in Ghana in 1929, James Barnor opened his renowned Ever Young studio in Accra, where he documented a nation at the moment of its independence. He was one of the first photojournalists to work with The Daily Graphic , a newspaper published in Ghana by London’s Daily Mirror Group. In 1959, two years after Ghana’s independence, Barnor moved to London to deepen his technical knowledge of photography. He discovered colour photography at Medway College of Art, and his pictures were published on the front page of Drum , an important magazine founded in South Africa in 1951 and a symbol of the anti-apartheid movement. He captured the spirit of Swinging London and the experiences of the African diaspora in the British capital. In the late 1960s, he was recruited by Agfa-Gevaert and returned to Ghana to establish the country’s first colour laboratory. He remained in Ghana for the next 20 years, working at his new Studio X23 as a freelance photographer and for state agencies in Accra. Today, Barnor lives in the United Kingdom and devotes much of his time to his work and passing on his knowledge. His photographs are held in institutional collections around the world, including the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA), Tate, the Victoria and Albert Museum, the National Portrait Gallery, the Centre Pompidou, the Musée du quai Branly – Jacques Chirac, the Detroit Institute of Arts, the National Gallery of Art in Washington, DC, and Photo Elysée.

items.title: Dangote, African bourses explore wider access for $1.6bn refinery IPO
items.description: By Yinka Kolawole, with agency repor t Dangote Group has held talks with African stock exchanges to broaden access to the $1.6 billion initial public offering (IPO) of its refinery beyond Nigeria, although differences in regulatory requirements across markets have complicated the process. Edoh Kossi Amenounve, Chief Executive Officer of the Abidjan-based Bourse Régionale des Valeurs Mobilières (BRVM), disclosed this in an interview with Reuters on the sidelines of the Africa Financial Summit in Luanda. Amenounve said discussions began in April at the invitation of Dangote Group, focusing on how stock exchanges across the continent could participate in the IPO despite differences in listing regulations. “It was not easy to have a kind of consensus on how the IPO can be conducted in all these different markets,” he said. He explained that one option under consideration was the use of Global Depositary Receipts (GDRs), which would allow securities representing Dangote refinery shares to be listed on other African exchanges. He cited similar arrangements in Kenya and Botswana. The refinery’s IPO, which closed on October 28, attracted subscription demand of about N6.4 trillion ($4.77 billion) from Nigerian retail and institutional investors, approximately three times the value of shares offered, according to people familiar with the transaction who spoke to Reuters. The shares are expected to be listed on the Nigerian Exchange (NGX) later in November. Amenounve noted that companies seeking listings across multiple African markets currently have to obtain separate approvals from the securities regulators in each jurisdiction, a process he said could be eased through regulatory harmonisation and mutual recognition. “If you want to ease this kind of process, maybe it is time to think about harmonisation and mutual recognition,” he said. He added that the technological infrastructure for cross-border securities trading was already available through the African Exchanges Linkage Project (AELP), but regulatory barriers continued to impede its full implementation. Meanwhile, Amenounve disclosed that BRVM had postponed the launch of West Africa’s first derivatives market to 2027 due to outstanding regulatory and technological requirements. Initial products are expected to include forward contracts on market indices and selected stocks. “The future of the continent is also in mining, agriculture, industrialisation, energy,” he said. items.title: FCCPC seals firms as oil, salt samples fail fortification tests
items.description: By Olasunkanmi Akoni The Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC) has sealed manufacturing facilities of defaulting food companies after laboratory tests revealed that 12 per cent of vegetable oil and two per cent of salt samples sold in Nigerian markets failed to meet mandatory micronutrient fortification standards. Executive Vice Chairman of FCCPC, Tunji Bello, disclosed this yesterday while presenting findings from a two-month market survey conducted in partnership with the Global Alliance for Improved Nutrition (GAIN), which exposed gaps in compliance with Nigeria’s food fortification policy, raising concerns over consumers’ access to essential nutrients through everyday food products. The survey examined 200 randomly selected samples, comprising 100 vegetable oil and 100 salt products collected from households and open markets across Northern and Southern Nigeria. Laboratory analysis revealed that 12 per cent of vegetable oil samples and two per cent of salt samples were inadequately fortified with essential micronutrients at household level. Of the 100 vegetable oil samples, 49 were unbranded, while 51 were branded products. The investigation also uncovered poor adoption of digital traceability systems for monitoring fortified food products along the supply chain. Only six vegetable oil manufacturers had registered on GAIN’s Digital Fortification Quality Traceability Plus platform, while three companies uploaded a combined eight product test results. Bello said large-scale food fortification was a mandatory public health policy aimed at tackling micronutrient deficiencies through the addition of essential nutrients, including vitamin A, iron, folic acid, zinc and iodine. He stated: “Consumers must be able to trust the quality of the products they buy and the health benefits those products are advertised to provide. “Consumer protection goes beyond resolving everyday complaints or halting deceptive business practices. It fundamentally comes down to ensuring that citizens are not denied the essential value, safety and nutritional benefits they pay for in the marketplace.” He said compliance directives had been issued to defaulting manufacturers, stressing that every batch of food products must meet established quality and safety standards. Bello added that the survey findings had been forwarded to the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC) for further regulatory action under the existing memorandum of understanding between both agencies. items.title: Trump blames Democrats’ midterm wins for US stock market plunge
items.description: US President Donald Trump has blamed the stock market’s sharp decline on the electoral victories recorded by the opposition Democratic Party in the midterm elections earlier this week. Trump made the accusation on Thursday in a post on his Truth Social platform, following a sharp selloff in US equities. “The Stock Market crashed today because the Dumocrats had a big Tuesday — So sad to see, you only have yourselves to blame!” he wrote. However, market analysts attributed the selloff largely to concerns that Democratic electoral gains could threaten investments in artificial intelligence (AI) data centres, amid growing opposition to such projects across the United States. The technology-focused Nasdaq recorded its worst percentage decline in a single session since April 2025. Data centre projects have faced opposition from voters across party lines, with several candidates who won seats in the midterm elections pledging to restrict or slow down their development. The Democrats made significant gains, flipping seats previously held by Republicans in South Carolina, North Carolina, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Texas and Maine. In Maine, former logger Troy Jackson defeated longtime Republican Senator Susan Collins, securing the party’s seventh Senate seat captured from Republicans. In Kansas, Methodist minister Adam Hamilton became the first Democrat elected to the Senate from the traditionally conservative state since 1932, while Iowa elected a Democratic senator for the first time since 2008. In Texas, Democrat Talarico declared that he had defeated “Goliath” after winning a Senate seat, while Gina Hinojosa unseated Republican Governor Greg Abbott, ending decades of Republican control of the governorship. Democrats also retained key Senate seats, including that of Jon Ossoff in Georgia, as well as an open seat in New Hampshire. Their gains extended to Michigan, where Abdul El-Sayed defeated former Republican lawmaker Mike Rogers, becoming the first Muslim elected to the upper chamber of Congress. In the House of Representatives, Democrats recorded gains across Pennsylvania, Kentucky, Arizona, North Carolina, Wisconsin and New Jersey, including districts Trump had won comfortably in 2024. In one closely watched contest in Indiana, Democrat J.D. Ford defeated Republican Congresswoman Victoria Spartz in a district Trump had carried by 17 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election. The Democrats also won Georgia’s governorship, with former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms making history as the state’s first Black woman governor. Republicans, however, secured victories in Florida, where Trump-backed Byron Donalds became the state’s first Black governor, while Ashley Moody retained a Senate seat after overcoming a strong Democratic challenge. items.title: PTI expresses concern over Imran's health, urges CJP to ensure court orders on treatment are implemented
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The PTI’s core committee has expressed concern over jailed party founder Imran Khan’s health, urging the chief justice of Pakistan to ensure the effective implementation of court orders regarding the ex-prime minister’s treatment. The party’s core committee met on Thursday and the gathering continued late into the night. It was held after reports that Imran’s blood pressure recently surged to 192 . A statement issued after the meeting said the committee had expressed “grave concern” over Imran’s health, citing the alleged lack of medical facilities and obstacles to his access to family members and personal physicians. The committee was briefed about Imran’s recent meeting with his lawyer, Salman Safdar, and termed reports about the surge in his blood pressure “extremely alarming”. “The core committee unanimously resolved that protecting Imran Khan’s health and life is an urgent humanitarian issue, and that any negligence, delay or irresponsibility in this regard is unacceptable. His health should be treated as a serious humanitarian and medical emergency rather than merely a political or legal dispute,” the statement read. It added that the committee demanded that the government provide Imran’s personal physicians with “immediate, unhindered and effective access” to him, make arrangements for all necessary medical examinations and diagnostic tests for Imran without delay, and transfer him to Shifa International Hospital for a complete medical evaluation and treatment. Noting that Imran had been in jail for over three years and concerns had been raised about his health, the committee resolved that any further delay in the fulfilment of its demand would be “unacceptable”. “The core committee appealed to the entire Pakistani nation, including overseas Pakistanis, to raise their voices immediately and forcefully to protect Imran Khan’s life and health. The meeting stressed that the gravity and urgency of this issue should be highlighted at the national and international levels,” the statement read. The committee appealed to the chief justice of Pakistan to ensure effective implementation of court orders regarding Imran’s treatment and give the matter “immediate attention” in view of its “exceptional humanitarian importance”. “The committee made it clear that implementing court orders is a constitutional and legal responsibility of the relevant government and administrative bodies, and that this responsibility cannot be evaded under any circumstances,” the statement said. It added that the core committee urged all PTI lawmakers, party organisations and office-bearers to raise the issue of Imran’s health, treatment and rights with “full force in Parliament, provincial sssemblies and other relevant forums”. The committee also expressed concern over an incident involving jailed PTI Vice Chairperson Shah Mahmood Qureshi in prison, “his fall and the resulting impact on his health”. It called for the relevant courts, the government and the prison administration to immediately transfer Qureshi to a hospital and ensure his complete medical examination and necessary treatment. Imran has been imprisoned since August 2023. His health has deteriorated over the course of his prison sentence, prompting outcry from members of the party. His eye ailment — right central retinal vein occlusion — came to light in late January, following which he has been taken to hospital multiple times. On Aug 18, the Supreme Court directed the government to shift the jailed ex-premier to Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad, a day after the superintendent of the Adiala jail — where Imran is imprisoned — submitted a report to the SC on the ex-premier’s health condition. In the report, the jail administration said adequate healthcare facilities were being provided to the couple, with their health and well-being a priority. However, an annexure to the report stated that Dr Akhtar Ali Bandeshah of Pims examined him on Aug 1 and noted complaints of uncontrolled and fluctuating blood pressure, palpitations, headache and restlessness. The ex-premier had attributed his symptoms and stress partly to infrequent meetings with his wife, family and social contacts, as well as the absence of newspapers and TV. On Aug 10, the SC was informed, a medical board comprising Pims specialists also examined Imran after he complained of heaviness in the head and palpitations. It recommended a one-hour daily walk and relaxation in his prison routine, besides access to newspapers, magazines, television and books. The board also recommended more frequent interaction with immediate family members or his spouse, saying this could help control his anxiety and blood pressure. Subsequently, the court ordered his transfer to Shifa International Hospital. However, the government took the PTI founder to Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences, a government hospital, and subsequently transported him back to prison. At the time, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar had blamed “the security situation created by PTI workers on the way to and outside” the hospital for the diversion. The PTI has denied the allegations and accused the government of deliberately flouting the court’s orders.

items.title: Power supply plunges as gas shortage, water level worsen
items.description: By Udeme Akpan, Obas Esiedesa & Ediri Ejor There are indications that electricity supply to consumers nationwide has worsened, with Distribution Companies (DisCos) receiving 2,926 megawatts (MW), amid inadequate gas supply, reduced water inflows into hydroelectric reservoirs and other operational constraints. Data obtained from the Nigerian Independent System Operator (NISO) showed a distribution across the DisCos with Abuja, Benin, Eko, Enugu and Ibadan DisCos receiving 633MW, 264MW, 256MW, 253MW and 391MW, respectively. Similarly, Ikeja, Jos, Kaduna, Kano, Port Harcourt and Yola DisCos received 249MW, 146MW, 167MW, 173MW, 320MW and 74MW, respectively. Explaining the decline, NISO stated: “The limited availability of gas has constrained the capacity of affected thermal generating stations to operate at their available levels, while reduced water inflows into reservoirs have impacted the generation capacity of hydroelectric power stations.” The operator added that the constraints had reduced electricity allocations to DisCos, resulting in fewer hours of supply and increased load shedding across distribution networks. “Consequently, the reduction in available generation has affected the quantum of electricity allocated to Distribution Companies (DisCos) for onward supply to consumers, thereby resulting in reduced hours of electricity supply and increased load shedding across distribution networks,” it stated further. Similarly, the Federal Ministry of Power acknowledged the impact of the outages on households, businesses and public institutions, particularly in areas that had recently recorded improvements in electricity supply. A statement signed by Adeola Adelabu, Special Adviser (Media and Publicity) to the Minister of Power, the ministry said: “We recognise what every hour without power means for individuals, families and businesses, and we do not take it lightly.” The Ministry further said preliminary assessments showed that the disruptions were not caused by any major or systemic failure of the national grid. It explained: “They stem from maintenance and operational issues on parts of the power ecosystem, together with a decline in generation caused by constraints in gas supply to thermal power stations and reduced output from hydroelectric stations due to lower water inflows into reservoirs.” The ministry disclosed that the Minister of Power, Joseph Tegbe, was working with the Transmission Company of Nigeria (TCN), NISO and DisCos to resolve the operational constraints, accelerate ongoing maintenance and restore normal supply. Meanwhile, generation had recovered to 3,688.95MW as of the time of filing this report, indicating a possible improvement in electricity supply. The breakdown showed that Azura-Edo IPP contributed 437MW, Okpai 421MW, Afam VI 320MW, Delta 334MW, Shiroro hydro 295.90MW, Jebba hydro 245MW, Kainji hydro 214MW, Omotosho 174.90MW, Olorunsogo 157.50MW, Geregu 117MW and Egbin 111MW. Other contributors included Omotosho NIPP, 102.10MW; Zungeru, 160MW; Olorunsogo NIPP, 90.60MW; Afam III, 70MW; Dadinkowa, 20.25MW; Paras Energy, 81.70MW; Omoku, 33.80MW; and Trans-Amadi, 2.20MW. items.title: Education Ministry, Gates Foundation consider partnership to boost Ghana’s malaria research
items.description: The Ministry of Education and the Gates Foundation are exploring areas of collaboration to strengthen Ghana’s capacity to develop and deploy locally driven solutions in the fight against malaria. The discussions centred on building local expertise in emerging malaria-control technologies, particularly research into the development of malaria-free mosquitoes, alongside technology transfer and institutional capacity building. The commitment was reaffirmed by the Minister of Education during a meeting with a delegation from the Ghana National Research Fund (GNRF), led by its Board Chairman, Prof. Eric Yirenkyi Danquah, and the Gates Foundation, led by its Deputy Director for Malaria, Mr Bruno Moonen. Prof. Gordon Awandare, Pro Vice-Chancellor of the University of Ghana, underscored the need to equip Ghanaian researchers with the technical expertise and resources required to develop and adapt such technologies locally. The Education Minister said sustained investment in research, talent development and strong local institutions would be critical to advancing the proposed collaboration. He said the broader objective was to strengthen Ghana’s research ecosystem, reduce malaria transmission and support the country’s ambition of eliminating the disease.

items.title: UN Security Council adopts Pakistan-led statement urging diplomacy during wars
items.description: UNITED NATIONS: The UN Security Council on Thursday adopted a presidential statement initiated by Pakistan, calling on countries to continue diplomatic engagement even after the outbreak of armed conflicts and urging sustained efforts to secure ceasefires, prevent escalation and achieve lasting political settlements. The statement, titled “The Role of Diplomacy during Active Hostilities”, emphasises that diplomatic engagement remains essential during wars to protect civilians, contain violence, prevent conflicts from spreading and facilitate humanitarian assistance. It urges countries to use mediation, good offices and direct or indirect communication between warring parties to ease tensions and create opportunities for negotiations, even as military operations continue. The statement was adopted under the November presidency of Latvia’s Ambassador Sanita Pavļuta-Deslandes, who is presiding over the Security Council this month. Pakistan’s Permanent Representative to the UN, Ambassador Syed Haider Shah, welcomed the adoption, describing it as an important contribution to international efforts to resolve conflicts peacefully. “The message of this Presidential Statement is both simple and powerful: Diplomacy must not end when hostilities begin. Indeed, it becomes even more indispensable,” he said during a press stakeout after the adoption. The Pakistani initiative builds on Security Council Resolution 2788, unanimously adopted during Pakistan’s presidency of the Council in July 2025, which reaffirmed the importance of a peaceful settlement of international disputes under the UN Charter. The latest statement extends that framework by focusing specifically on diplomatic engagement after armed confrontations have begun, a period when communication between opposing sides often breaks down and the risk of further escalation increases. The Council emphasised the importance of maintaining communication channels between parties to armed conflicts, both directly and through intermediaries. Such contacts can help prevent miscalculations, facilitate de-escalation and provide opportunities for political negotiations. “Through good offices, open channels of communication and continued dialogue, diplomacy can provide a vital bridge from confrontation to de-escalation and peaceful settlement,” Ambassador Shah said. The statement also identified several practical objectives for diplomatic engagement during active hostilities, including facilitating cessations of hostilities, ensuring safe and unhindered humanitarian access, protecting civilians and reducing the danger of conflicts widening into regional or international confrontations. It further emphasised that ending hostilities should not be an end in itself, stressing that diplomatic and political engagement must continue after a ceasefire to secure a lasting political settlement. The statement also recognised the contribution of individual UN member states that undertake diplomatic initiatives during armed conflicts. It encouraged them to continue using mediation, good offices and diplomatic engagement to reduce tensions and facilitate transitions from confrontation to peaceful resolution. Regional and subregional organisations are also identified as important contributors to conflict resolution. The Council welcomed efforts to strengthen their mediation capacities and encouraged closer cooperation between them and the United Nations. The statement further highlighted the role of the UN secretary-general in using his good offices, along with those of his representatives, special envoys and UN mediators, to promote dialogue and peaceful settlements. It encouraged the secretary-general to continue supporting diplomatic efforts before and during armed conflicts, including initiatives aimed at de-escalation and sustainable political solutions. The Council also reaffirmed that diplomatic efforts must remain consistent with the UN Charter, international law and relevant Security Council resolutions. It recognised the role of other UN organs in supporting peaceful dispute settlement, including the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in adjudicating disputes where states have consented to its jurisdiction. Ambassador Shah said the adoption brought together the Council’s experience in dealing with individual conflict situations under a common thematic framework, providing a political reference point for diplomatic initiatives in ongoing and future conflicts. “Today’s adoption represents a meaningful contribution to the Council’s thematic body of work,” he said. He added that the initiative reflected Pakistan’s commitment to multilateralism, dialogue and the peaceful settlement of disputes. The Council also requested the UN Secretary-General to continue promoting diplomacy, mediation and peaceful dispute resolution and keep it informed, as appropriate, of efforts in this regard.

items.title: Tinubu has shown he cares about workers with ₦70,000 allowance — Oshiomhole
items.description: Senator representing Edo North, Adams Oshiomhole, has said President Bola Tinubu has demonstrated concern for workers’ welfare through the Federal Government’s approval of a ₦70,000 monthly transport allowance. Oshiomhole made the statement during an interview on Channels Television’s Politics Today on Thursday, where he defended the Tinubu administration’s performance and urged Nigerians to appreciate its policies. “I think this government is doing well. If a man who was on ₦70,000 now is given ₦70,000 addition that makes it ₦140,000 for him it’s a hundred percent increase and if you know what ₦10,000 means for the real masses, you’ll appreciate that Tinubu has shown that he cares,” he said. The Federal Government approved the monthly ₦70,000 transport intervention for workers across all levels for six months, beginning in November 2026, following a meeting with the Nigeria Labour Congress (NLC) on October 27. The agreement also provides for the payment of outstanding peculiar allowances in three equal monthly instalments beginning in November. However, the Trade Union Congress (TUC) rejected the transport allowance, insisting that workers need a permanent salary increase rather than temporary relief. Oshiomhole also criticised the administration of former President Olusegun Obasanjo, under which Atiku Abubakar served as vice-president, alleging that it failed to guarantee the payment of workers’ salaries. He said the 2027 presidential election would offer Nigerians a choice between Tinubu, whom he credited with unifying the exchange rate, and Atiku, whom he accused of allowing multiple exchange rates that favoured people based on their connections. The senator also faulted the presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi, for allegedly failing to present an alternative to Tinubu’s policies. “Peter Obi has not offered any alternative. I’ve always said that Peter Obi is a trader; the logic of a trader is short term turnover. A statesman that Tinubu represents thinks of the next generation,” Oshiomhole said. While acknowledging the right of opposition candidates to contest the presidency, he argued that Tinubu should be allowed to continue in office after “having gone through all the teething problems” rather than “recruit a new apprentice.” The post Tinubu has shown he cares about workers with ₦70,000 allowance — Oshiomhole appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: IPOB demands release of detained Igbo men, alleges persecution
items.description: ….Group says release of four men after four years in DSS custody exposes alleged injustice By Chimaobi Nwaiwu NNEWI — The Indigenous People of Biafra (IPOB) has demanded the release of Igbo people it claims are being unlawfully detained across correctional facilities in the country, alleging continued persecution of Ndigbo. The group said the recent court-ordered release of four Igbo men, who were reportedly held in the custody of the Department of State Services (DSS) for almost four years, exposed what it described as systemic injustice against the people. IPOB, in a statement by its Media and Publicity Secretary, Emma Powerful, titled, “The Persecution of Biafrans Must End: A Demand for Accountability and Rule of Law,” said the release of the four men should not be mistaken for a resolution of the wider concerns over the detention of its members. The group said its legal team had identified 83 people allegedly transferred from military custody at Wawa Barracks in Kainji, Niger State, to correctional facilities in Kuje, Keffi and Suleja. It claimed that its lawyers had communicated the names of legal representatives for the detainees to the Office of the Attorney-General of the Federation. IPOB further alleged that several other people remained in detention, with some reportedly serving life sentences over cases linked to alleged membership of the group. Describing the situation as an abuse of state power, IPOB argued that political association or alleged membership of the organisation should not constitute grounds for imprisonment without proof of specific criminal offences. The group also questioned the legal basis of its proscription, arguing that the process was conducted through a civil ex parte proceeding and lacked the statutory approval required from the President under Section 2(1)(c) of the Terrorism (Prevention) Act 2013. It maintained that the signature of a Chief of Staff could not substitute for presidential approval where such approval was expressly required by law. IPOB cited the judgment in MultiChoice Nigeria Ltd v. FCCPC, involving Justice James Omotosho, to argue that statutory requirements should be applied consistently, irrespective of the parties involved. The group also referred to what it described as a subsisting inter partes ruling that IPOB was not an unlawful society, insisting that the government and prosecuting authorities should address the legal implications of the ruling. It disclosed that an appeal concerning the organisation’s status and the legality of its proscription was pending before the Supreme Court. IPOB argued that no individual should be sentenced to life imprisonment solely on the basis of alleged membership of the organisation, insisting that prosecutors must establish specific offences against each defendant. The group called on the Federal Government to account for the 83 people it said had been identified in correctional facilities in Keffi, Suleja and Kuje, as well as other people allegedly being held in connection with the Biafran agitation. It also urged the United Nations, the United States Government and the European Union to intervene over what it described as violations of the rights of detained Biafrans. “The release of the four is not the end of the matter. It is an indictment of the system that kept them imprisoned for four years,” the statement said. IPOB demanded the release of all people it considers unlawfully detained and an end to what it described as the criminalisation of its membership.
