items.title: Hardship: Northerners turn to cargo trucks for cheaper journeys despite risks
items.description: By Maryam Abdul-Aziz Usman, Damaturu POTISKUM — Despite Dangote’s ban on unauthorised passengers, Northerners still board its trucks to escape rising transport fares. In July 2026, Dangote Industries Limited offered N500,000 for credible information on illegal haulage, including unauthorised passenger transport, but travellers in Potiskum say rising fares leave them with few affordable options. Baba Iyatu, a middle-aged woman, was perched atop a Dangote compressed natural gas (CNG)-powered truck, among dozens of other passengers preparing to leave Potiskum, Yobe State. Her destination was Niger State, where her daughter had just given birth. For her, the journey was about family. But with the cost of conventional transport increasingly difficult to afford, reaching her daughter meant accepting the uncertainties of travelling on a truck designed to carry goods, not passengers. Baba Iyatu and the others knew the company prohibited unauthorised passengers on its trucks. Yet they argued that those enforcing the restrictions did not understand their economic circumstances. To them, the arrangement offered cheaper travel while giving drivers and their assistants opportunities to earn extra money. Their predicament captures a troubling reality in Nigeria: when the price of moving from one place to another becomes prohibitive, some people are willing to sacrifice comfort and safety to reach their destinations. The difference in cost is stark. Lagos fare A transport union worker known as agbero (name withheld), was interviewed at the ‘Tashan Na Tsira’ Motor Park in Potiskum, and he told the Arewa Voice correspondent that a bus journey from Potiskum to Lagos, which previously cost about N15,000, now costs approximately N35,000. By comparison, passengers can negotiate rides on heavy-duty trucks for between N5,000 and N10,000, depending on the driver’s mood. The difference can amount to as much as N30,000 on a single journey. For people already struggling with the cost of food, accommodation and other necessities, that saving can determine whether a journey is possible at all. Fuel prices have compounded the problem. In September 2026, petrol prices reached around N1,400 per litre in parts of Nigeria and N1,500 in some northern locations, while diesel exceeded N2,000 per litre, according to Reuters. Rising fuel costs add to the expenses facing transport operators, who must also contend with maintenance, spare parts and other running costs. But the passengers negotiating rides at Potiskum’s ‘Baban Tasha Park’ are not all travelling for the same reasons. Their stories reveal how the informal use of cargo trucks intersects with family obligations, unemployment and commercial activity. ‘I’ll think about job when I ge to Lagos’ Among those preparing to travel to Lagos was Adamu Hamisu, 24, who had secured a place on a privately owned truck transporting beans to the commercial city. It was his first trip to Lagos. He had arranged to stay with a friend but had no definite business plan. Asked what business he intended to start, Adamu said he would think about it once he arrived. For the young man, reaching Lagos came before deciding what to do there. He was travelling in search of greener pastures, hoping that being in the city would bring opportunities he could not readily access at home. His journey illustrates the uncertainty facing young people who leave their communities to seek work or start businesses without substantial resources. Spending less on transportation could leave them with more money for food, accommodation and the first steps towards earning a living. Hassan Idris, 34, was travelling for a different reason. The livestock trader was taking 14 rams to Lagos to sell. He had arranged with the truck driver to collect a few more animals in Azare, Bauchi State. Having traded livestock for five years, he already had accommodation arrangements in Lagos and middlemen who bought his animals for resale. Unlike Adamu, who was heading towards an uncertain future, Hassan was moving within an established commercial network connecting livestock traders in northern Nigeria with buyers in southern markets. Their journeys demonstrate how the use of cargo trucks extends beyond people simply trying to save money. The vehicles also form part of the wider movement of goods, traders and economic activity between communities. For the drivers and their assistants, however, the economics of the practice are different. Iliya, a truck driver’s assistant, explained that truck owners receive payment for delivering goods, while drivers and their assistants are settled for food and ‘calculated fuel expenses’. The assistants help deliver the cargo but do not necessarily receive the main payment for the job. Carrying passengers therefore offers another possible source of income. Sama’ila Ado, a truck driver who drove into ‘Tashan Yawale’, explained that drivers and their assistants also make money from selling used engine oil. According to him, the additional earnings form part of the informal arrangements through which they try to meet their daily needs while transporting goods over long distances. These accounts expose the competing pressures surrounding the practice. The truck owner has a commercial delivery to complete; the driver and assistant must manage the journey’s expenses; and passengers are looking for a cheaper way to travel. An arrangement that benefits one party financially, however, does not automatically make it safe or permissible. The dangers begin with the conditions in which passengers travel. Those riding in open truck compartments or perched atop cargo have little protection from rain, dust and harsh weather. They also face the risks associated with sudden braking, vehicle instability and road accidents. For Baba Iyatu, the journey was a means of reaching her daughter and newborn grandchild. But the emotional importance of that visit could not remove the physical risks of travelling in a vehicle designed to carry goods rather than people. Drivers also contend with difficulties that can make long-distance haulage more expensive and unpredictable. Sama’ila described bad roads, rain and encounters with people who block roads and demand money from drivers. Such accounts point to additional pressures on transport operators, although the locations and circumstances of the reported incidents require further verification. Poor road conditions can delay deliveries, increase vehicle maintenance costs and leave drivers exposed to breakdowns far from assistance. For operators already managing fuel and food expenses, delays and unexpected payments can further complicate the economics of a journey. Dangote’s rule on truck Dangote’s restrictions add another dimension to the problem. In July 2026, Dangote Industries Limited (DIL) announced a whistleblowing initiative offering N500,000 for credible information leading to action against the unauthorised use of its branded trucks, including the transportation of unauthorised goods and passengers. The company said the initiative was intended to protect its logistics operations and ensure that its trucks carried only approved cargo. The company also said law enforcement agencies, including the police, had been authorised to arrest drivers found using its trucks for unauthorised commercial haulage. The presence of passengers on the Dangote-branded truck observed in Potiskum therefore raises questions about how the restrictions are enforced and why some travellers continue to accept the risks. The observation establishes that passengers were aboard the truck; it does not, by itself, establish the identity of the truck’s operator or whether the company was aware of that particular journey. For passengers, the immediate concern is the price of reaching their destinations. For the company, unauthorised use of its vehicles raises questions of compliance, operational control and liability. For road safety authorities, transporting people in cargo compartments presents risks that cannot be dismissed simply because the fares are cheaper. Nigeria’s road safety figures underline the wider danger. The Federal Road Safety Corps recorded 10,446 road crashes and 5,289 deaths nationwide in 2025, according to figures reported by the News Agency of Nigeria. These national figures do not establish how many crashes involved passengers on cargo trucks, but they demonstrate the serious consequences of road accidents. In Potiskum, the stories of Baba Iyatu, Adamu Hamisu, Iliya and Sama’ila touch on a question that a company ban alone cannot answer: why are people willing to take the risks of travelling on cargo trucks? One woman wants to see her newborn grandchild. One young man hopes to find a future in Lagos. A livestock trader is taking animals to established buyers. Drivers and their assistants are seeking additional earnings while completing deliveries. Their circumstances differ, but all are connected by the economics of the open road. Al’baru travel may offer immediate savings, but it also exposes passengers to hazards associated with vehicles not designed to carry them. The challenge is not simply to enforce restrictions on unauthorised passengers; it is also to understand the economic pressures that make the practice attractive. Until safe, affordable transport becomes more accessible, the gap between the cost of travelling legally and the cost of taking a cargo truck may continue to push people towards journeys that save money but place their safety at risk. items.title: Eight killed, 30 injured in bus-truck collision on Hazara Motorway
items.description: ABBOTABAD: At least eight people were killed and 30 others injured when a passenger bus collided with a dumper truck near the Havelian Interchange on the Hazara Motorway early Friday morning, rescue officials said. The bus was travelling from Gilgit to Rawalpindi when the accident occurred. Initial reports suggested that a tyre burst caused the driver to lose control of the vehicle before it collided with the truck, the Rescue 1122 statement said. Following the incident, Rescue 1122 Abbottabad dispatched seven ambulances and a rescue vehicle to the scene to carry out relief operations. The rescue operation, led by District Emergency Officer Hafeezur Rehman, was completed successfully. Rescue personnel provided first aid to the injured before shifting them to nearby hospitals for treatment. The bodies of the eight deceased, who reportedly belonged to Gilgit, were transported to different hospitals. One body was taken to Type-D Hospital in Havelian, while four were shifted to Ayub Medical Complex and three to the District Headquarters Hospital (DHQ) Abbottabad/ All 30 injured passengers, including five children and six women, were shifted to Ayub Medical Complex for medical treatment. The condition of four injured passengers was reported to be critical, added the statement. A day earlier, a collision between a passenger bus and truck claimed the lives of 11 people and left 33 others injured near Pakpattan. Last week, at least five people were killed and 27 others injured when a passenger bus plunged into a drain in Punjab’s Hafizabad district.

items.title: High Court Ruling: AA candidate warns against weakening opposition
items.description: By Ibrahim Hassan-Wuyo The presidential candidate of the Action Alliance (AA), Faduri Oluwadare Joseph, has warned that increasing judicial involvement in political party disputes could undermine democratic participation and weaken opposition politics ahead of the 2027 general elections. Joseph, popularly known as Fadojoe, expressed concern over the implications of the Federal High Court judgment concerning the leadership of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) and the presidential nomination of former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar. In a statement issued under his Operation Rescue Nigeria 2027 platform, the AA candidate said the judgment had raised questions about the independence of the judiciary, the future of political competition and the state of Nigeria’s democracy. He said his intervention was not motivated by membership of the ADC but by the need to protect democratic participation and the right of Nigerians to freely choose their leaders. According to him, an injustice against democratic participation in one political party could eventually affect other parties and candidates. “Today, it is Atiku Abubakar and the ADC. Tomorrow, it could be Peter Obi, myself, or any other opposition candidate,” he said. Joseph maintained that although political parties and candidates must operate within the law, the judiciary should ensure that its decisions did not undermine the fundamental principles of democratic participation. He expressed concern over what he described as a growing trend of political parties spending more time in courtrooms defending their leadership structures and electoral rights than presenting their programmes to Nigerians. The AA candidate also questioned the increasing influence of internal party disputes, prolonged litigation and conflicting judicial interpretations on the electoral process. He argued that courtrooms should not become substitutes for ballot boxes, insisting that the judiciary must protect justice and public confidence in the democratic process. Joseph further raised concerns about the state of opposition politics under President Bola Tinubu’s administration, citing persistent leadership disputes, factional disagreements and legal battles involving opposition parties. He noted that the ADC had accused the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) of attempting to weaken the opposition through legal processes, but stressed that such allegations required independent examination. The presidential candidate urged Tinubu and the APC to recognise the importance of a strong opposition in sustaining democratic governance. He recalled Tinubu’s involvement in the pro-democracy struggle against military rule, particularly the activities of the National Democratic Coalition (NADECO), arguing that democratic freedoms should be protected regardless of political affiliation. Joseph said the rights and freedoms demanded by pro-democracy activists during the military era should also be guaranteed to those opposing the present administration. He warned that Nigeria’s democratic system could be weakened if opposition parties and their candidates were unable to compete freely in elections. items.title: 2027: Peter Obi is a trader, he hasn’t offered any alternative — Oshiomhole
items.description: Senator representing Edo North, Adams Oshiomhole, has described the presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, Peter Obi, as a trader who has failed to present an alternative to President Bola Tinubu’s policies ahead of the 2027 general election. Oshiomhole made the remarks during an interview on Channels Television’s Politics Today on Thursday, arguing that Obi’s approach to governance was driven by short-term gains rather than long-term national development. “Peter Obi has not offered any alternative. I think it is you or someone else who asked him for security, what will you do differently? He said, it’s in his heart. “I’ve always said that Peter Obi is a trader; the logic of a trader is short term turnover. A statesman that Tinubu represents thinks of the next generation,” he said. The former Edo State governor said he respected the right of opposition candidates to contest the presidency but maintained that Tinubu deserved another term after overcoming the initial challenges of his administration. According to Oshiomhole, Nigerians should allow the President to continue rather than “recruit a new apprentice”. He also criticised the administration of former President Olusegun Obasanjo, under which former Vice President Atiku Abubakar served, alleging that it failed to guarantee the payment of workers’ salaries. The senator framed the 2027 election as a choice between Tinubu’s economic policies and those of Atiku, whom he accused of presiding over a system of multiple exchange rates that favoured people based on their connections. Oshiomhole defended the Tinubu administration’s workers’ welfare policies, citing the approval of a ₦70,000 monthly transport allowance as evidence that the President cared about ordinary Nigerians. “I think this government is doing well. If a man who was on ₦70,000 now is given ₦70,000 addition that makes it ₦140,000 for him it’s a hundred percent increase and if you know what ₦10,000 means for the real masses, you’ll appreciate that Tinubu has shown that he cares,” he said. The Federal Government approved the monthly ₦70,000 transport intervention for workers across all levels for six months, beginning in November 2026, following a meeting with the Nigeria Labour Congress on October 27. The agreement also provides for outstanding peculiar allowances to be paid in three equal monthly instalments beginning in November. However, the Trade Union Congress rejected the transport allowance, arguing that workers need a permanent salary increase rather than temporary relief. items.title: Paraguay president resigns amid Ueno Bank crisis
items.description: Paraguayan President Santiago Peña has reportedly resigned amid a political crisis following the collapse of Ueno Bank, a digital lender allegedly linked to his former business interests. Peña announced his resignation on Thursday in a video message posted on social media, saying his decision was intended to protect the country’s stability, social peace and democratic institutions. “I want to apologise to the people if at any point I failed. It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me,” he said. According to Reuters, the resignation followed moves by Paraguay’s lower house of Congress to pursue impeachment proceedings against Peña over allegations of conflict of interest and misconduct relating to the bank. Peña has denied any wrongdoing, rejecting suggestions that his previous business relationship with Ueno’s owner influenced his conduct as president. Ueno Bank was reportedly placed under resolution by Paraguay’s Central Bank earlier in the week after regulators found that its solvency ratio had fallen below the required minimum. The intervention reportedly affected the accounts of about three million customers, leaving many unable to access their savings and other funds. The bank had also administered hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds, including pension and other government resources, Reuters reported. The development triggered protests in the capital, Asunción, with demonstrators demanding Peña’s resignation. Authorities subsequently began arrangements to compensate affected depositors, while reports indicated that eight Ueno executives had been detained and their assets frozen as investigations into the bank’s operations widened. Peña was said to have been a shareholder in Grupo Vázquez, the company that previously owned Ueno Bank, until 2025. Opposition lawmakers had accused him of a conflict of interest over his previous relationship with the bank’s ownership and the government’s dealings with the lender. The president, however, maintained that he had committed no wrongdoing. In his resignation message, Peña called on authorities to protect public funds and ensure that affected customers recovered their money. “I want the affected people to be guaranteed the return of those resources, that the Deposit Guarantee Fund fulfil its purpose and that public funds and resources belonging to all Paraguayans be protected,” he said. His reported resignation came after the resignation of Paraguay’s central bank governor earlier in the crisis. Reuters reported that Vice-President Pedro Alliana was expected to assume the presidency following Peña’s departure. items.title: Accra’s disturbing potholes endanger motorists
items.description: Some major roads and highways in Accra have developed serious potholes, making driving on those roads dangerous for motorists and other road users. Motorists who use these roads frequently indicated that their repeated calls to the authorities to fix the potholes have fallen on deaf ears, leaving them to navigate the damaged stretches at their own risk. Abeka Lapaz A visit by MyJoyOnline to some of the affected areas showed the extent of the problem and the daily struggle drivers go through to avoid damage to their vehicles or accidents. At the Abeka Lapaz interchange, a portion of the busy outer lane had developed a deep pit. Drivers say the pothole keeps breaking car axles and forcing them to swerve suddenly into other lanes, a situation that could easily cause accidents, especially during rush hours. On the UPSA road On the UPSA road, near the University of Ghana Business School, several potholes have also developed. The road, which is used by students, lecturers, and residents, has become difficult to drive on, with motorists slowing down to avoid the damaged portions. At East Legon, on the American House main road, there are also potholes. The area is one of the busiest commercial and residential zones in Accra, and drivers say the potholes cause heavy traffic congestion as vehicles queue to dodge them. At the Sakaman Junction traffic light, on the Accra-Kasoa Highways, there is another dangerous pothole. Motorists say the pothole is particularly risky because drivers who stop at the traffic light are forced to move over it when the light turns green, causing damage to tyres and suspensions. Similar potholes were also found at the New Bortianor and West Hills Mall area, where drivers say the road has deteriorated badly and needs urgent attention. Many motorists who spoke during the visit expressed frustration over the state of the roads. East Legon They said they spend huge sums of money repairing their vehicles due to damage caused by the potholes, while others expressed fear for their safety, especially when driving at night or rainy days. The potholes are filled with water and are difficult to identify when there is a downpour. They are therefore appealing to the Ghana Highway Authority, the Department of Urban Roads, and the Accra Metropolitan Assembly to urgently repair the potholes before they cause serious accidents and loss of life.

items.title: Key takeaways from 32nd Nigerian Economic Summit
items.description: By Emeka Anaeto, Business Editor The 32nd edition of Nigerian Economic Summit held last week in Abuja has produced one of the most critical insights and engagements across stakeholders in Nigeria’s economy spanning across public and private sector. It also delivered some thought provoking contents on what is wrong with economic development in the country across policy strategies and execution imperatives. With significant dose of international personalities with experiences across the world, the discussions were frank and unpatronising of any vested interest. Themed, ‘‘Growth that Works: Delivering Jobs, Productivity and Shared Prosperity’’, the cardinal objectives were anchored on the three-and-half years of President Bola Tinubu’s massive economic reform which has already become controversial ahead of the next general elections in the country. The gathering of distinguished global leaders, senior government officials across the Federal and State levels, private sector executives, economists, and development partners were set to build consensus on practical pathways for accelerating inclusive and sustainable growth. The NES#32 actually provided platform for translating reform momentum into tangible outcomes that could expand productive employment, raise productivity and ensure shared prosperity. Furthermore, the Summit dissected Nigeria’s development priorities across five critical sub-themes, including: Work Nigeria, which entails building a job-rich and strengthening labour absorption; Produce Nigeria, which entails driving productivity, industrialization, and value creation; Invest Nigeria, which entails delivering investment, shared prosperity, welfare, and social protection; Scale Nigeria , which entails expanding growth across states, sectors, and communities; and Secure Nigeria which entails restoring safety, stability, and confidence for economic activities. The key takeaways from the 32nd Nigerian Economic Summit show the outcome reinforced one overriding national imperative: ‘Nigeria must move decisively from macroeconomic stabilisation and policy reform to measurable economic prosperity, productive employment and improved living standards for its citizens’. The discussions acknowledged progress towards macroeconomic stability while emphasising that growth must translate into improved household incomes, greater business competitiveness, food security, stronger institutions and broader economic opportunities. Reforms performance presents a mixed picture – NESG Chairman Welcoming the array of Nigerian business elites at the thirty-second edition of the Nigeria Economic Summit in Abuja yesterday, the Chairman of NESG, Mr Niyi Yusuf, said though the reforms have presented a form of stability but he declared that stabilization may create conditions for economic progress but doesn’t deliver it. Dissecting the major outcomes from the reforms so far, Yusuf stated: “Nigeria’s economic performance presents a mixed picture. Key macro indicators are improving, but significant constraints limit the transmission of these gains to businesses and households. He further noted, “Nigeria attracted approximately US$23.2 billion in foreign capital inflows so far in 2026, but portfolio investment dominated, with foreign direct investment only a small proportion. Giving NESG’s overall position on the performance of the reforms so far, Yusuf stated: “These reforms have imposed considerable pressures on households and businesses, but they have also created an opportunity to reconsider the foundations of our socio-economic development. “Our responsibility now is to ensure that reform translates into stronger enterprises, better jobs, more productive workers, rising incomes, improved living standards and shared prosperity. This is the central purpose of NES #32. No other way than reforms – Tinubu Speaking to the global audience about the reforms’ imperatives and deliveries, President Bola Tinubu, through his deputy, Vice President Kashim Shettima, said the administration is currently undertaking what it came into office to achieve: rewriting the story of a nation that has performed below its potential for far too long. ‎He noted that his administration began on a difficult note because there is no shortcut to economic growth. These reforms are restoring confidence, strengthening our economic foundations and laying the groundwork for sustainable growth,” he added, noting that the administration is encouraged by what it has accomplished so far. ‎”We must judge industrial policy by the competitiveness of our firms and investment incentives by the capital, technology, exports and jobs they attract.” ‎On economic diversification, he stated that “non-oil activities accounted for 96.08% of GDP, while manufacturing grew by 3.29% and the oil sector by 2.57%,” emphasising that the gains have reinforced his administration’s confidence in the path of recovery and diversification. ‎Giving more performance highlights of the administration the President stated: “In the first quarter of 2026, our capital importation reached $10.37 billion, an increase of 83.83% over the corresponding period in 2025. This comprised both portfolio and foreign direct investment. We will, therefore, continue to ease regulatory burdens, strengthen transparency and policy predictability, and expand access to finance. Conditions for Nigeria to achieve sustainable economic growth – Prof Dercon Speaking on how Nigeria could move from economic stabilisation to sustained growth, Professor Stefan Dercon of the University of Oxford, United Kingdom, who delivered the keynote speech, stated: ‘‘For Nigeria to achieve sustainable economic growth, its political, business, military and civil service elite must forge a common front, abandon the status quo and commit to a development agenda’. that serves the broader national interest. Dercon warned that the process would not be easy because those benefiting from the existing system were likely to resist changes that threatened their interests. He said Nigeria needed a coalition of influential groups committed to economic expansion, peace and stability, rather than a system that primarily protected the interests of a privileged few. 10 strategic outcomes From the deliberations documented, ten strategic outcomes and priorities emerge: 1. A New Economic Accord for Inclusive and Sustainable Growth: The Summit underscored the need for a durable economic accord that institutionalises reforms beyond political and electoral cycles. Discussions called for stronger policy consistency, improved federal–state coordination, export-led growth and increased productive investment. The objective is to move beyond economic growth of approximately 4% towards the 7–9% growth considered necessary to accelerate poverty reduction, while raising investment from approximately 17–20% towards 30–40% of national output. 2. Accelerating Trade Competitiveness and Regional Integration: The Summit identified trade facilitation as essential to unlocking the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA). Priorities include modernising ports, reducing border delays, introducing one-stop border posts, improving multimodal logistics and removing non-tariff barriers. Particular emphasis was placed on developing competitive regional value chains in agro-processing, pharmaceuticals, building materials and light manufacturing, alongside stronger market access for MSMEs and women traders. 3. Unlocking MSMEs and the Informal Economy: A central message was that Nigeria’s informal economy should be treated as a productive national asset rather than merely a regulatory challenge. The discussions advocated incentive based formalisation, affordable and appropriately structured financing, stronger industrial supply-chain linkages, improved market access and sustained business-development support. MSME interventions should be data-driven, responsive to different business growth stages and institutionalised for continuity. 4. Strengthening Subnational Fiscal Sustainability and Investment: The Summit highlighted the critical role of states in translating national economic stability into local prosperity. Recommendations focused on broadening internally generated revenue through improved administration rather than excessive taxation, strengthening expenditure efficiency, institutionalising fiscal transparency and developing bankable public-private partnership projects. Greater use of subnational bonds, blended finance and climate financing was also recommended, supported by credible governance and accountability arrangements. 5. Making Security a Foundation for Economic Growth: The Summit established a clear connection between insecurity, agricultural productivity, investment decisions, supply-chain disruption and food inflation. Discussions supported intelligence-led and locally responsive security arrangements, stronger coordination between public institutions and businesses, and sustainable security financing. The proposed state policing framework received particular attention, with emphasis on professional standards, independent oversight, citizen protection and safeguards against political interference. Importantly, the NESG reaffirmed its commitment to advancing public-private security collaboration through its Human and Business Security Roundtable. 6. Advancing Digital Inclusion, Productivity and Responsible Artificial Intelligence: The Summit recognised digital transformation as an opportunity to expand productivity, employment and economic participation. Priorities include interoperable government digital infrastructure, affordable rural connectivity, employment-linked digital skills, responsible artificial intelligence and stronger digital platforms for small businesses. The central outcome was the recognition that digital inclusion must be measured not simply by connectivity, but by improvements in productivity, incomes and access to opportunities. 7. Transforming Education, Skills and Human Capital: The discussions identified weaknesses in foundational learning, significant numbers of out-of-school children and persistent mismatches between education and labour-market requirements. Recommendations included modernising curricula, expanding technical and vocational education, strengthening industry-led training and linking skills development to employment opportunities. The Summit also called for coordinated private-sector investment in education through mechanisms such as the Business Coalition for Education, results-based financing, stronger state partnerships and measurable human capital outcomes. 8. Mobilising Innovative Finance for Transport and Trade Infrastructure: The Investment Partnership Lab highlighted opportunities to mobilise strategic international partnerships for transport connectivity, inland waterways and the blue economy. Priority proposals included feasibility and navigability studies, phased development of the SeaLink Corridor, dedicated cargo terminals and stronger inter-agency coordination. The discussions also identified European Union technical assistance and a proposed sovereign blue bond of US$500 million before 2030 as potential mechanisms to advance bankable infrastructure investment. These remain proposals and financing objectives identified in the discussions, rather than confirmed financing commitments. 9. Aligning Fiscal and Monetary Policies with Household Prosperity: The Summit emphasised that monetary and fiscal stability must support productive enterprise, lower financing costs and improved household welfare. Recommendations addressed domestic revenue mobilisation, tax compliance, transparency in public spending, credible communication of economic reforms and stronger support for small producers. The discussions reinforced the importance of public trust and accountable spending in sustaining reform implementation. 10. Institutionalising Implementation, Accountability and Shared Responsibility: Across the sessions, a consistent priority emerged: moving from policy discussions to coordinated execution and measurable results. The Summit advocated stronger government–business partnerships, clear institutional responsibilities, evidence-based interventions, transparent reporting and performance monitoring. The expectation is that government, businesses, development partners and citizens should contribute to a common economic transformation agenda, with progress assessed against tangible development outcomes. The overarching message The central message emerging from the Summit is that economic stability is necessary, but it is not sufficient. Nigeria’s next phase of development must be defined by the quality of growth, the competitiveness of its enterprises, the resilience of its institutions and the opportunities available to its citizens. The deliberations have provided a clear direction for advancing this transformation through policy consistency, productive investment, regional integration, human capital development, improved security and accountable institutions. items.title: Prof Beyuo takes responsibility for medical bills of 12 injured in Hamile unrest
items.description: Lambussie MP Professor Titus Beyuo has offered to pay the hospital bills of 12 people injured in the violence that erupted in Hamile following a deadly explosion in the Upper West Region. The injured residents are receiving treatment at different health facilities, with two requiring surgery for fractures sustained during the disturbances. The other 10 are said to be stable and awaiting medical reviews to establish whether they are fit for discharge. The injuries followed confrontations between some residents and security personnel after tensions rose over allegations that civilians had been shot. The situation reportedly escalated into protests targeting the Ghana Immigration Service. During the unrest, some protesters allegedly destroyed an Immigration Service checkpoint, damaged about three vehicles and moved towards the service’s office, prompting security personnel to secure the facility. Warning shots were reportedly fired during the confrontation, leaving 12 people with injuries. Ten sustained puncture wounds, while two suffered fractures. A bullet was subsequently removed from the limb of one of the injured residents. The two patients with fractures were transferred to the regional hospital after nearby facilities were found unable to provide the required treatment. Speaking on Citi FM on Thursday, November 5, 2026, Prof. Beyuo said he had visited the injured residents and informed their families and the hospitals that he would settle the cost of their treatment. “I’ve informed the hospitals where they are, visited them, and I’ve informed the doctors there to give all the care and then forward the bills to me to settle,” he said. The MP said the incident had created an unexpected situation for the affected families and assured them of his support as the residents receive medical attention.

items.title: Game Review — I love and loathe the mixed bag that is Modern Warfare 4
items.description: TL;DR Pros: Gunplay feels amazing with the removal of random weapon spread Animation and visual quality is superb Campaign has a compelling story, good voice acting and solid mission design Multiplayer maps are good overall, with Silkworm being a standout Every weapon in the game feels like a viable option DMZ is a decent third mode Cons: Requires a persistent internet connection Installation was a pain Skill-based matchmaking NEEDS TO BE REMOVED Major issues with lag and connection DMZ can be unforgiving, thanks to players camping exfil points Apex attachments are mostly gimmicky rather than genuinely useful Score: 5/7 — one of the better entries in years, but still a long way from the golden age. Reviewed on PlayStation 5; available on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, PC and Nintendo Switch 2. Price: Rs20,000 (physical copy); $69.99 ( digital ) All GIFs and screenshots captured by author A few months ago, I expressed my hesitation about whether or not I would be willing to buy this year’s Call of Duty after playing the open beta. While gunplay improved massively, the maps were solid, and it felt like a good CoD game again, these were offset by a very, very badly implemented skill-based matchmaking (SBMM) system, “innovations” with little practical benefit, and poor network code and lag issues. Now the full game is here, and we can really determine whether this is a return to form or another slap in the face like last year’s Black Ops 7 ( BO7 , or “Black Slop 7”). Modern Warfare 4 ( MW4 ) is neither: it’s a step in the right direction, but repeats the mistakes that sent the franchise into a downward spiral to begin with. This really is the definition of a mixed bag, but is it worth your money? Going dark. Rs20,000 of inconvenience Before we go anywhere, I really need to address the issues I came across while installing the game. CoD has this really odd system when it comes to installation on console: your disc has none of the game on it and simply acts as confirmation that you own the game. You have to download and install the CoD launcher first, then Multiplayer, Campaign and DMZ as individual content packs. Aside from the fact that these downloads take a while, you can’t access anything else while one part of the game is downloading. I installed Multiplayer and played a couple of hours before downloading DMZ. Anyone else remember the days when the full game was on a disc? When the latter began installing, I couldn’t access multiplayer to pass the time. The entire game was locked off. Campaign: It held the line CoD campaigns are a big deal for me, and last year’s campaign was easily the worst in the entire franchise. The bar was literally on the ground and developers Treyarch were still unable to step over it. Random side note: I have never seen anyone unironically use ‘YOLO’ in at least 15 years. My expectations for MW4 were pretty much nonexistent, and when the trailer came out, I thought it looked cool, but that was about it. Series creator Infinity Ward took the reins and gave us a story in an underutilised setting: a present-day conflict in the Korean Peninsula. The North invades the South in a strong enough introduction — a patrol in a South Korean city with your squad is upended by hypersonic missiles. Picked the wrong time to go for a walk. What follows is a desperate scramble to hold off North Korean forces as Private Park, a grunt in the Republic of Korea (ROK) Marines. This modern interpretation of the Korean War is truly superb in its grounded and gritty tone, and showing it through the eyes of a Korean rather than an American made it much more immersive. Park’s squad has very good chemistry, with dialogue feeling organic in both its writing and delivery. Similarly, North Korean officer Ko Jin-Hyuk and Commander Ri Ju-Young, one of the antagonists, stood out because of their expressive performances and Ko’s character arc. Actors Lanny Joon and Prisca Kim deserve a round of applause, even if in Ri’s case the writing was a bit cartoonish and a stereotype of what the West thinks North Korea is really like. Ko is a real one, and a great inclusion to the franchise. Meanwhile, series mainstay Captain Price is chasing after someone called “The Archer”, who is played by Danish actor Mads Mikkelsen. Again, superb acting, even though I’d have liked more screen time from the latter. This B plot occurs several days before the invasion, showing the buildup before converging with the Korean campaign, Pulp Fiction -style. There are even bits where you take control of North Korean soldiers to flesh out the game’s world, albeit reinforcing the stereotype. In terms of gameplay, the campaign succeeds where MW3 and BO7 dropped the ball; it delivers a coherent story and well-designed missions and levels. You aren’t dumped in a gigantic, empty level that bores you to death; levels are linear and serve a purpose, such as a John Wick-esque nightclub gunfight, a beach landing on the Korean Peninsula and searching for defectors in a North Korean village. These immerse the player and provide a focused experience. The one time you do end up in a giant, open level, effort has been put in. The mission ‘Stranded’ puts you in the North Korean wilderness scavenging supplies, gear and weapons to strike three facilities. Though the level is massive, it’s populated with enough enemies to not feel empty, and enough activities to keep you meaningfully occupied. It can, however, get monotonous if you’re trying to complete everything and find every secret. Even Captain Price thinks it’s absolute cinema. Multiplayer: Fun, but frustrating This is the component I’ve spent the most time with so far, and it’s largely standard fare when it comes to CoD: fast, reflex-driven action on small maps with two teams of six. For the most part, I’m genuinely enjoying it. Maps, characters and guns have a very high level of detail, and the animations, particularly weapon handling, continue to lead the industry. The open beta in August showcased some of this already, but it’s still no less impressive. This is my rifle. There are many like it but this one is mine. Aesthetically, the maps vary quite a fair bit and are generally appealing, with one or two exceptions. ‘Sentry’ is a snowed-in military facility with grey walls and a very muted colour palette. It’s a decent map to play in, but it looks boring. On the other side of the spectrum, ‘Silkworm’, set in a South Korean city, is vibrant and has more visually diverse locations like internet cafes and convenience stores. I’ve wracked my brain and can’t think of a map I didn’t like. They’re all well-crafted, funnelling the action into certain areas while being easy to learn. However, my complaints about formulaic map design still stand — they all have three clearly defined lanes, only one storey of height and few routes for flanking, limiting how you can play the game. Silkworm is easily my favourite. Gunplay feels rock solid, with weapon bloom — the randomness in the spread of your bullets — completely removed, and the sound design really helps them sound and feel beefy. Unlike other games in the franchise, each weapon in the arsenal feels like a viable option, especially the pistols. The Apex for the Han 86 assault rifle with integrated airburst grenade launcher. Forget what I said earlier. THIS is my rifle. Some weapons are used more widely than others, but for the most part, I’ve noticed that everything is being used by the player base. However, the Apex attachments introduced in the game fall flat. A few of them, like ammo conversions, can be truly useful, but the vast majority serve little to no use in your loadout. You’ll use them once for a laugh, and then just get back to business with standard weaponry. Now, we have to address the elephant in the room: skill-based matchmaking , or SBMM . For those unfamiliar, it is a system of matching players based on individual performance rather than internet connection and it creates a twofold problem: because connection is not prioritised, issues like lag emerge; and since it finds players based on your performance, if you play well, it’ll match you with guys playing like it’s the finals of the CoD world championships. It’s an extremely controversial feature that completely sucks the fun out of not just CoD , but multiplayer games in general. I shouldn’t be punished for getting a high score by being pitted against either professional players or the chronically unemployed. One good match will be followed up by another with players of a far higher skill level who have mastered every trick in the book. I just want to unwind with my friends after work, not put up with lag or players sweating over their keyboards and controllers, playing hard. Removing SBMM completely would make the game so much better and address a lot of community backlash. I’d go a step further and say it should be banned under international law. My face when the SBMM kicks in. DMZ: In and out, 20-minute adventure DMZ is an extraction mode and the third main component of the MW4 package, returning after its introduction in 2022’s MW2 reboot. You enter the zone, complete missions, grab gear and leave via one of several exfiltration points. However, the stakes are high: death or disconnection means all of the stuff you picked up is gone. All of it. It’s a tense experience, pitting you against AI-controlled enemies and other players in a race to get high-tier loot, weapons, gear and other equipment to help you survive. To its credit, there is a lot of stuff to do in the DMZ, with story missions, dynamic operations — small side missions to make some money and earn some gear — and other activities like hunting lieutenants and taking down minibosses roaming the map. One of the better ways to get around Hajin. The main map, Hajin, is massive and atmospheric, with abandoned buildings, North Korean iconography everywhere, varying architecture and plenty of elements to explore. There’s even a dynamic weather system in place, with a sunny day turning into a rainstorm in real time. It’s a departure from the other modes seen in CoD, which I’m a fan of, even if it’s very unforgiving, especially against enemy players. However, there are issues here. The time-to-kill compared to multiplayer is minuscule, with an enemy player shredding through your armour almost instantly. Since I mostly dealt with AI bots who are slow to react, it leaves me ill-prepared for a player moving like a rocket-propelled kangaroo. Call it a skill issue if you want; it’s just plain irritating. There would have been many more items here had I not suffered a disconnect. I would love a bots-only option here, so that I don’t have to worry about someone waiting for me to exfiltrate, then stealing my stuff after catching me by surprise. Again, connection issues plague this mode; a couple of nights ago, I completed a very cool mission where you have to extract a North Korean general from a hospital — pushing him in the world’s most heavily armoured hospital bed to a helicopter — only for the game to disconnect before I could exfiltrate, sending all of my hard-earned, high-level loot to the abyss. There is no word in any language to describe how angry I was. There must be some workaround to this problem. No joke, the Mirae Hospital extraction mission is pretty good. Love and loathe I’m torn on MW4 ; it brings back a lot of what made the franchise so beloved to begin with: a fast-paced, addictive multiplayer and an engaging single-player campaign. It’s a major improvement, while also paying homage to the original Modern Warfare trilogy. However, there are many problems with this entry, which make it frustrating to deal with, from matchmaking to poor servers. Despite this, I’ve found myself going back to it regardless. As a package, I loved my time with this, faults and all, and I play almost every night. This is not a return to form; it’s nowhere near close to the original trilogy, but it is a step in the right direction, albeit one with a twisted ankle. Time to squad up with the boys again, see you for the next review, folks.

items.title: Pourquoi la Chine publie-t-elle 7 fois moins de séries statistiques qu’il y a dix ans ?
items.description: En 2012, le Bureau national des statistiques de Chine publiait chaque année plus de 80 000 séries statistiques aussi variées que les effectifs du secteur des équipements pour aires de jeux en plein air, la production nationale de sauce soja, la surface des toilettes des écoles primaires ou le bilan électrique de la Mongolie-Intérieure. En 2022, ce chiffre est tombé à seulement 11 000 China’s GDP blackout isn’t fooling anyone », Financial Times , 21 octobre 2022.'> 1 . La difficulté d’accéder à ces statistiques contribue à l’opacité croissante du régime chinois, qui cherche à contrôler au maximum l’accès des acteurs étrangers à ces signaux utilisés pour mesurer le développement et la prospérité du pays. Plus de 20 000 de ces séries ont notamment cessé d’être publiées entre 2019 et 2022, pendant la pandémie de Covid-19. Officiellement, le régime n’a reconnu qu’environ 81 000 décès à l’hôpital durant la vague de l’hiver 2022-2023, alors que des études indépendantes estiment la surmortalité à entre 700 000 et 1,9 million de personnes et al. , « Excess mortality in Mainland China after the end of the Zero COVID policy : A systematic review », Epidemiology and Infection , 22 décembre 2025.'> 2 . Faute de pouvoir se fier aux chiffres officiels, les chercheurs ont depuis plusieurs années recours à des indicateurs de substitution, comme l’intensité lumineuse nocturne captée par des images satellites, pour tenter d’estimer la croissance du PIB du pays. Un économiste étudie notamment le nombre d’articles de presse consacrés aux propriétaires de salles de sport et de salons de beauté qui ferment en empochant l’argent des abonnements, afin d’évaluer la santé du secteur des services How Bad Is China’s Economy ? The Data Needed to Answer Is Vanishing », The Wall Street Journal , 4 mai 2025.'> 3 . La Chine n’est pas le seul pays à avoir fortement restreint l’accès à ses séries statistiques. En Russie, Rosstat a notamment suspendu la publication de plusieurs séries de données démographiques : nombre de naissances, de décès, de mariages, de divorces, ainsi que leur ventilation par région. Le démographe russe Alexeï Rakcha estime que, depuis mars 2025, « il n’y a pratiquement plus de statistiques démographiques publiques en Russie ». Depuis son retour au pouvoir, Donald Trump a également mis fin à la publication de plusieurs séries, dont certaines dans le sillage de ses décrets sur le genre et sur la diversité, l’équité et l’inclusion : origine ethnique et genre des fonctionnaires fédéraux, nombre d’Américains souffrant de la faim, coût des catastrophes météorologiques ou relevés de qualité de l’air des capteurs installés dans les ambassades et consulats américains American federal data has a zombie problem », Not-Ship , 28 octobre 2026.'> 4 . Selon le Federal Data Terminations Tracker, 38 jeux de données ont été supprimés et 337 éléments de données retirés au 28 octobre – un décompte que sa cofondatrice juge sous-estimé Federal Data Terminations Tracker , [consulté le 5 novembre 2026].'> 5 . L’opacité sur la santé de l’économie chinoise sert à Pékin à contrôler le récit : sans accès libre aux données, il est difficile de mesurer le choc provoqué par l’effondrement du secteur immobilier, d’évaluer l’état des finances des gouvernements locaux ou de comparer le chômage des jeunes avec celui du reste du monde. Au-delà des séries statistiques, le régime chinois a aussi drastiquement raccourci les biographies officielles des hauts responsables politiques et des fonctionnaires. Alors que le pouvoir a accéléré sa purge de l’Armée populaire de libération en 2025, le manque d’informations sur les profils et les parcours des dirigeants du Parti et de l’armée complique la lecture des transformations en cours à Pékin. Le CSIS a recensé 62 généraux et lieutenants-généraux purgés ou disparus en 2025, dont 15 officiellement, contre 11 l’année précédente et 14 en 2023. L’article Pourquoi la Chine publie-t-elle 7 fois moins de séries statistiques qu’il y a dix ans ? est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: Fani-Kayode, Seyi Tinubu, three others receive Senior Counsel rank
items.description: By Chidinma Chukwu, Abuja Nigeria’s High Commissioner to South Africa, Lesotho and Eswatini, Chief Femi Fani-Kayode, and four other legal professionals have been conferred with the rank of Senior Counsel of Nigeria (SCN) by the Nigerian Law Society (NLS). The conferment took place at the society’s 2026 Annual General Conference, themed, “Justice for All: Non-Litigation Nigerian Law Graduates Through the Blue Silks (SCN), BOSCON and the NLS”. The other recipients are Seyi Tinubu, Olufunmilayo Osifuye, Ihudiebube Chukwumdi and Alabi Olalekan Adigun. In his acceptance speech, delivered by his Special Adviser on Media and Executive Assistant, Mrs Lizzy Okoji, Fani-Kayode called for greater protection of the rights and dignity of Nigerians, both within and outside the country. He stressed that access to justice must not be determined by an individual’s social, economic or political standing. “Justice in its truest form must never be selective. It must not be reserved for the privileged, the powerful or the politically connected. It must be accessible to all,” he said. Reflecting on his diplomatic assignment in South Africa, Fani-Kayode said the experience had reinforced his commitment to human rights, particularly in view of the challenges confronting Nigerians in the country. He recalled that his first official engagement upon arriving in South Africa was a town hall meeting with members of the Nigerian community, where he listened to their concerns and reassured them of the Federal Government’s commitment to protecting Nigerians abroad. According to him, the promotion of human rights requires courage, compassion, sacrifice and an unwavering commitment to truth. The NLS President, Ambassador Dahiru Aliyu, said the society was established to provide an organised platform for Nigerian law graduates whose professional engagements extend beyond courtroom litigation. He listed corporate administration, legal consultancy, arbitration, mediation, compliance, governance, legislative drafting and research among the professional fields covered by the society. Aliyu disclosed that the NLS was established alongside the Body of Senior Counsel of Nigeria (BOSCON), with its certificate of registration obtained on December 30, 2025. He said the initiative was established in accordance with Section 40 of the 1999 Constitution, as amended, which guarantees freedom of association. On the Blue Silks initiative, the NLS president said it was designed to recognise professional excellence, dedication and outstanding contributions to the legal community, while encouraging younger law graduates to embrace professional ethics and continuous development. He listed his administration’s priorities to include institutional consolidation, membership expansion, continuing professional education, financial accountability and stronger national and international partnerships. Aliyu also urged members to uphold transparency, comply with the society’s constitution and resolve disagreements through dialogue and lawful dispute resolution mechanisms. In her keynote address, the BOSCON Chairperson, Hon. Mrs Elizabeth Titilayo Orebiyi, represented by Mrs Ndidi Nicholas Okoro, said legal practice and professional development were not limited to courtroom advocacy. She highlighted the contributions of law graduates in universities, corporate organisations, legislative chambers, regulatory institutions and policy development, noting that these areas offered significant opportunities for legal professionals outside traditional litigation. Orebiyi identified four categories under the Blue Silks initiative as Senior Legal Academic (SLA), Senior Corporate Counsel (SCC), Senior Legislative Counsel (SLC) and Senior Law Reform Counsel (SLRC). She said the Senior Counsel designation should reflect experience, competence, integrity, intellectual leadership and service to society. “A Senior Counsel should be a mentor, a custodian of professional values and an example to those who follow,” she said. She also encouraged younger law graduates to develop expertise in emerging areas of legal practice, including technology, artificial intelligence, commercial innovation, regulatory transformation, international transactions and alternative dispute resolution. Also speaking, the Chairperson of the NLS Physical Planning and Building Control Appeals Committee, Olufunmilayo Osifuye, advocated fairness and accountability in everyday relationships and professional engagements. Osifuye, who heads a committee responsible for hearing appeals relating to planning permits and building control in Lagos State, clarified that the NLS was not established to compete with the Nigerian Bar Association (NBA). “We are not competitors to other arms of the legal profession, but complementary to their work because we serve the same goal,” she said. The Public Relations Officer of the NLS Ogun State Branch also urged members to uphold the rule of law, promote peaceful coexistence and protect human dignity. The post Fani-Kayode, Seyi Tinubu, three others receive Senior Counsel rank appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Opoku-Agyemang calls for prosecution of perpetrators of sex-for-jobs abuse
items.description: Vice President Professor Jane Naana Opoku-Agyemang has called for prompt investigations into sexual exploitation allegations in workplaces and educational institutions, stressing that anyone found guilty must be appropriately sanctioned. She warned that demands for sexual favours in exchange for employment opportunities or academic grades were damaging to Ghana’s development, depriving institutions of talent, weakening productivity and undermining public trust. The Vice President made the call at the 2026 Sex for Jobs Conference in Accra, where she described the practice as an abuse of authority that violates personal dignity and compromises the integrity of workplaces and educational institutions. “The exploitation known as sex for jobs in workplaces and sex for grades in academic and training institutions constitutes an abuse of power, an erasure of bodily autonomy, and a breach of institutional integrity,” she said. Professor Opoku-Agyemang said the consequences went beyond the immediate harm to victims, noting that such misconduct also carried significant economic and social costs. “Beyond the moral injury, these are economic and social costs, including lost productivity and wasted talent. Every instance of abuse that forces people into silence erodes public trust in the institutions established to serve those people,” she added. She said government acknowledged the scale of the problem and its responsibility to ensure that allegations were properly addressed. She further advocated independent and confidential reporting mechanisms to protect complainants, particularly in cases where the accused persons wield authority over victims’ recruitment, promotion or academic progression.

items.title: 2027 UTME: JAMB threatens substandard CBT centres, sets tough accreditation conditions
items.description: By Joseph Erunke Abuja -The Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board, JAMB, has moved to tighten its grip on the conduct of the 2027 Unified Tertiary Matriculation Examination, UTME, warning that computer-based test (CBT) centres that fail to meet its prescribed standards will be denied accreditation. The Board said only centres with adequate facilities, reliable infrastructure and the operational capacity to guarantee a credible and hitch-free examination would be approved to host candidates in the 2027 exercise. JAMB Registrar, Prof. Segun Aina, gave the indication during a meeting with the leadership of the Chief External Examiners, where preparations and readiness for the accreditation exercise ahead of the 2027 UTME were reviewed. According to a post on the Board’s official X handle, yesterday, the meeting was part of efforts to strengthen examination administration and ensure strict compliance with established operational standards. The Board said the accreditation exercise would serve as a critical screening mechanism to prevent inadequately equipped centres from participating in the examination, thereby protecting candidates from avoidable disruptions and compromising examination conditions. “Only centres that meet JAMB’s standards will be accredited to host the examination. For candidates, that means a fair and secure place to sit the UTME, wherever they write it,” the Board stated. The development signals JAMB’s determination to strengthen the credibility of the UTME by ensuring that candidates, irrespective of their examination locations, have access to a secure, reliable and conducive testing environment. items.title: Assafuah rejects Mahama’s invitation to World Cup visa probe committee
items.description: Member of Parliament’s Youth and Sports Committee Ranking Member, Vincent Ekow Assafuah, has rejected an invitation to appear before a committee set up by President John Dramani Mahama to investigate alleged irregularities in the 2026 FIFA World Cup visa acquisition process. The MP says he will not participate in an investigation whose independence he questions, insisting that the allegations should instead be examined by an independent commission of inquiry. At a press conference on Thursday, November 5, Mr Assafuah disclosed that the invitation was conveyed to him by the President through his presidential advisers. He argued that the president’s involvement in the process raised concerns because the investigation could involve ministers serving in his government. “I have respectfully boycotted that invitation. I did so on principle. The president cannot be seen to be investigating his own ministers. You cannot be a judge in your own cause,” he said. Mr Assafuah also faulted the committee for what he described as a lack of openness, questioning why its membership, terms of reference and proceedings had not been made public. “That committee is shrouded in complete opacity. Its terms of reference are not public, its members are unknown, and its sittings are held behind closed doors,” he said. He disclosed that he had petitioned the Office of the Special Prosecutor and the President to establish an independent commission to investigate the alleged visa and fundraising irregularities. According to him, such a commission should operate transparently, have the power to compel the production of evidence and make its findings available to the public. “What Ghana needs is not a secret in-house cover-up committee. What Ghana needs is a public, transparent, independent commission of inquiry with powers to subpoena, to publish evidence and to hold persons accountable openly,” he added.

items.title: Mahama sets monthly review of road crash data to measure TraffiTech results
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama says the government will use monthly road accident figures to determine whether the newly introduced TraffiTech system is reducing crashes and preventing deaths on Ghana’s roads. He said accident data recorded after the system became operational on November 1, 2026, would be compared with figures from the corresponding months last year to establish its impact. Addressing a meet-the-press session at Jubilee House on Thursday, November 5, the President appealed to motorists to observe speed limits, particularly the 50-kilometre-per-hour limit in urban centres, as the government steps up automated traffic enforcement. Mr Mahama said the technology was intended to improve compliance by replacing manual speed checks by police officers with an automated system that detects speeding and provides evidence of offences. He expressed confidence that the intervention would help reduce road fatalities, citing 2,151 people killed in road crashes in Ghana last year. Of that number, 474 were pedestrians knocked down by vehicles, with schoolchildren returning from school accounting for a significant proportion of the deaths. The President said excessive speed makes it difficult for drivers to respond quickly when pedestrians cross roads unexpectedly, increasing the likelihood of fatal collisions. “I can assure you, if we bear with this TraffiTech system, when you see the results of reduction in accidents at the end of the year, because it started November 1st, we’ll do a month-to-month comparison with last year,” he said. “And you yourself will be surprised at the number of lives this TraffiTech system will save.” He reiterated that motorists in urban areas, including Accra, must not exceed 50 kilometres per hour, adding: “The general speed limit in any urban centre, including Accra, is 50. And so you are not supposed to go above 50.” Mr Mahama also clarified that the speeding detection component is the only part of the TraffiTech system currently in operation.

items.title: Asia stocks tumble after AI rout rocks US markets
items.description: A rout in Asia’s tech-heavy markets deepened on Friday as fear of increased regulatory scrutiny and a slowdown in AI build-out precipitated the steepest decline in US stocks since the tariff-triggered “Liberation Day” selloff in April 2025. Japan’s Nikkei slumped 7 per cent immediately after the opening bell while benchmark share price indices in South Korea and Taiwan dropped more than 8pc. Stocks across the region then appeared to stabilise as dip buyers emerged. European stock futures also cut initial loss and were last down 0.6pc. Nasdaq futures were up 1.4pc though sentiment remained fragile. Wall Street’s volatility “fear gauge” soared, the Nasdaq sank 5.5pc and $3 trillion was wiped off S&P 500 firms, with investors worried Democrats, who dominated midterm elections this week, will apply brakes to the AI boom. The political jitters are hitting an AI trade already on shaky footing due to worry about return on companies’ enormous investment in artificial intelligence-related infrastructure. “There is also clearly an element of panic in the selling, and positioning is making the adjustment much more violent,” said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo. “When investors begin unwinding these positions simultaneously, the selling can become self-reinforcing, particularly if leverage and forced liquidations are involved.” The meltdown spooked retail investors and hedge funds alike, while policymakers and regulators scrambled to stem the selling. AI chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix fell nearly 10pc and 12pc respectively in South Korea. Kioxia plunged 14pc in Japan while TSMC fell as much 8.5pc in Taiwan. AI investor SoftBank Group slid 11pc, while the cost of insuring against the Japanese firm defaulting on debt jumped to its highest in four years. “The selloff shows that AI stock prices had been built on rosy illusions about the future, and now that illusion is gone,” said Dong Baozhen, chairman of asset manager Lingtong Shengtai. “The US stock market has been the standard-bearer and backbone of the global AI bull run. Now that backbone has snapped. Can AI bull markets elsewhere hold up on their own?” Sentiment shifts, cracks emerge Investor fear also centred on whether a stalling AI infrastructure expansion could hurt smaller firms whose capacity to raise funds has already been limited by higher interest rates and tighter financial conditions. Neocloud firm CoreWeave, which has become a barometer of investor anxiety over heavy AI spending and borrowing, slumped 10pc, while its five-year credit default swap spreads widened to a record level. “It’s pretty clear there’s been a real shift in sentiment,” said Michael McCarthy, chief executive for Australia and New Zealand at brokerage Moomoo. The selling indicates investors are starting to factor in increased local opposition to data centres, with analysts saying markets have yet to fully consider the cost such building has imposed on communities. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index slumped 12.2pc overnight and the Nasdaq, which reversed an initial swing higher after the midterms before dropping, has now shed 12pc from its record close a month ago. Still, some analysts said the selloff was overdone and the bottom was not far off. “Today we are bound to see further liquidation of margin accounts, which suggests we are likely in the final stage of capitulation,” said Allen Huang, a vice president of Mega Financial Holding’s equities trading department. “Even TSMC hit its daily limit down circuit breaker at one point, which typically marks the tail end of a downturn. When TSMC gets sold off, that means all stocks have been thoroughly dumped,” Huang said. Finding refuge in bonds and Yen Bonds gained in Asia, with US Treasuries as well as government bonds in Japan and China rising, while the US dollar slipped against haven currencies such as the yen and Swiss franc. “Treasuries can probably rally a lot further,” said Nick Ferres, chief investment officer at Vantage Point Asset Management. The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note was at 4.838pc, hovering near the lowest level since September 9. The 10-year JGB yield dropped as much as 9 bps to 1.795pc, the lowest since June 30.

items.title: Car dealers block Kwashieman footbridge walkway, exposing pedestrians to danger
items.description: Roadside car dealers have blocked the pedestrian walkway leading to the Kwashieman footbridge in Accra, making it difficult for pedestrians to cross the N1 highway. The dealers, who have been operating alongside the highway, have now extended their activities onto part of the walkway to the footbridge. They have displayed cars for sale to cover almost half of the path, forcing pedestrians to struggle for space as they walk to and from the footbridge. The situation has forced pedestrians to cross the busy George Walker Bush Highway, where speeding cars pass almost every minute. The walkway was constructed to give pedestrians safe access to the footbridge and to protect them from the fast-moving vehicles on the N1. However, with cars now parked on the walkway, pedestrians are being pushed closer to the main road, exposing them to danger. Some pedestrians who use the footbridge daily say the situation is worrying, especially during rush hours when many people use the route to cross to the other side. According to residents, schoolchildren, the elderly and persons carrying loads are the most affected because they find it difficult to manoeuvre through the narrow space left by the parked cars. They are appealing to the Accra Metropolitan Assembly, the Ghana Highway Authority and the law enforcement agencies to intervene and remove the cars from the walkway. They say if the dealers are not stopped, they will completely take over the walkway and permanently force pedestrians onto the highway, which could lead to accidents and loss of life. The pedestrians are calling for regular enforcement to keep the walkway clear and safe for its intended purpose.
