items.title: Finance Minister applauds Nyakrom Community Bank for pioneering banking initiative
items.description: Dr Cassel Ato Forson, the Minister of Finance and Economic Planning, has applauded the Nyakrom Community Bank PLC for its pioneering initiative in Rural /Community banking. He said this had positively impacted the lives of the people in the communities and the country at large. The Finance Minister said the 50 years of excellent rural banking services were commendable, particularly as plans advanced to transition from rural to community banking, capturing the essence of financial institutions in their catchment areas. In a speech delivered on his behalf at a durbar to mark the 50th Anniversary celebration of the Nyakrom Community Bank PLC at Nyakrom in the Agona West District of the Central Region, Dr Forson noted that the inherent idea had finally been realised through the reforms of the Bank of Ghana (BOG), converting rural banks into community banks which deserved to be celebrated. It was on the theme: “50 years of rural banking in Ghana; celebrating the pioneering role of Nyakrom Community Bank PLC.’’ The Minister said, exactly 50 years ago, in 1976, the Government of Ghana in collaboration with the Bank of Ghana (BOG) introduced the rural banking concept as an antidote to the long-standing exclusion of rural Ghana from banking services. He said that before the introduction, rural communities in Ghana had limited access to credit, with financing coming mainly from informal savings, where money was often kept at home, while rural businesses remained underdeveloped. He said the community banking sector had now grown to 147 banks with about 1,000 branches nationwide and over 800,000 customers, playing a pivotal role in expanding access to credit, mobilising rural savings and supporting financial enterprises. He further noted that the sector had created thousands of jobs for the youth and improved rural and peri-urban livelihoods, a significant achievement deserving celebration. Dr Forson said the Nyakrom Community Bank had strategically grown from one to 11 branches with more than 350 staff and approximately 100,000 customers, and had, in the past four years, extended its operations to many regions in Ghana. The Minister stressed that as the banking industry continued to evolve and become more competitive with the conversion of rural banks into community banks, the banking landscape had become increasingly universalised, making the competition keener and fiercer. Dr Samuel Dufu, the inventor and pioneer of rural banking in Ghana, said the model was first introduced to the then Omanhene, the chiefs and other people of Nyakrom after he had explained the concept and its benefits to them. On conviction that the people had embraced the concept, a seven-member promotion team was formed, and they later became the board of directors of the bank. Dr Dufu said on July 09, 1976, Nyakrom Rural Bank was born as the first rural bank in Ghana and he was elected the first chairman of the board of directors. He stated that the first project the bank undertook was to redeem and return all cocoa farms ceded to moneylenders to their owners, bringing relief to the impoverished farmers. Dr Dufu said he remained the chairman of the board of directors of the bank for 30 years until 2006, nurturing it to grow from strength to strength, adding that rural banking was a calling and one needed a heart of love to man it. He stated that Consultants from the Philippines, Messrs SGV&CO, were commissioned in 1996 to study the situation of rural banks, and recommended that an apex institution be set up for the rural banks to provide technical, managerial and financial support. “My experience in rural banking during the past 50 years has taught me that any good project would endure and thrive when given the required commitment and nurturing,” he added. Nana Ambrose Linson-Arthur, the Board Chairman of Nyakrom Community Bank PLC, said the bank had offered 50 years of financial inclusion, self-reliance and community development. Farmers in cocoa, oil palm, cassava and vegetable production had been financed by the Bank and they were helping to feed the nation, while traders and SMEs in various markets were expanding their businesses and creating jobs. Nana Linson-Arthur said it had also provided school loans and educational support to parents and students and had partnered with health centres, churches and educational institutions through corporate social responsibility to provide infrastructural development. The bank is poised to deepen financial inclusion through agency banking, mobile money partnerships, launching of new products for women, youth and agribusiness, and investing in cybersecurity and digital platforms to make banking safer and faster. Mr Kaidebi Donkor, the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of Nyakrom Community Bank PLC, commended Dr Samuel Dufu, a native of Agona Nyakrom, together with the chiefs and other stakeholders, for establishing the first rural bank in Ghana. The CEO said the bank’s total assets as at August 2026 stood at GHC232 million, loans GHC 146 million, deposits GHC 203 million, and start up capital GHC 8.3 million far above the requirement of the BOG through its microfinance reforms framework 2026. Mr Donkor appealed to the finance minister and Parliamentarians to consider reducing the 30 per cent tax imposed on the profits of Community Banks because it was affecting their smooth operations. Other speakers were Dr Kwadwo Asmah, the CEO of Amenfiman Community Bank PLC, Alhaji Hayatudeen Awudu Ibrahim, the President, National Association of Community Banks, Madam Patience Antonio, President, Central Regional Chapter Association of Community Banks and Mr Curtis William Brentuo, the Acting Managing Director, ARB Apex Bank.

items.title: Japan Motors CEO Salem Kalmoni unveils his 6 rules for business success
items.description: Business mogul Salem Kalmoni says the lessons he has gathered from years of managing a family-owned enterprise have taught him that success depends as much on avoiding costly mistakes as it does on pursuing growth. He has distilled those lessons into what he calls the ‘ Six Bs of Business Success’ — a set of practical principles shaped by about 25 years of experience in the business. The principles, which he said were developed through repeated challenges and “bitter experience”, are: banish bad debt, banish dead stock, buy well and sell easy, be frugal, be best of friends with suppliers, and choose good brands. Mr Kalmoni outlined the six principles when he appeared on Joy FM’s Personality Profile with Lexis Bill on Thursday, November 5, saying entrepreneurs often concentrate on the achievements of successful businesses without paying enough attention to the difficulties and sacrifices behind them. “I’ve made so many mistakes in business. You often look at success; you don’t look to get to success what you’ve done, the difficulties and how much it cost us in this,” he said. He explained that some of the challenges he encountered occurred repeatedly, prompting him to reflect on the experiences and identify lessons that could guide business owners. “So much so that I put them all together, and I came out with the six B’s of business success,” he said, adding that the principles were arranged in order of importance. The first, banish bad debt, places emphasis on the need for businesses to manage credit carefully and avoid allowing unpaid obligations to undermine their financial position. His second principle, banish dead stock, draws attention to the cost of keeping goods that do not sell. Unsold inventory can tie up capital that could otherwise be used to meet operating expenses, replenish fast-moving products or pursue new opportunities. The third, buy well, sell easy, highlights the importance of making sound purchasing decisions. For businesses involved in trading, the price, quality and terms on which goods are acquired can determine how easily they can be sold and whether the transaction yields a reasonable return. Mr Kalmoni’s fourth rule is a call for discipline in spending and the careful use of business resources. He also urged entrepreneurs to be best of friends with their suppliers, stressing the value of maintaining strong relationships with the people and companies that provide the goods and services on which businesses depend. His final principle is to choose good brands — a reminder that the products and brands a business represents can influence its reputation and its ability to attract and retain customers. Mr Kalmoni said the six principles had emerged from his experience in the family business, rather than from a theoretical exercise. The lessons come from a family enterprise with a long history in Ghana’s trading and automotive sectors. The Kalmoni family’s business roots date to 1920, when his grandfather, the late Salem Kalmoni, established Kalmoni & Sons, initially operating in transport and trading. The business expanded into vehicle imports, bringing the first Japanese-made Datsun vehicle into Ghana in 1958. Japan Motors Trading Company emerged from the family enterprise in 1962 and was incorporated as a limited liability company in 1965. Mr Kalmoni, a third-generation member of the family, joined the company in 1991 after completing his studies in Canada. He later led its operations in Ghana before his appointment in 2026 as Group Chief Executive Officer of Japan Motors Network, which has operations in Ghana and other West African markets. His six principles offer a practical summary of the financial discipline, stock management, purchasing decisions, cost control, supplier relationships and brand choices that he considers essential to building and sustaining a business. He suggested that explaining the lessons in detail would require considerably more time, describing the subject as one for a full masterclass.

items.title: Belle semaine pour la Bourse de Casablanca
items.description: La Bourse de Casablanca a clôturé la semaine du 02 au 05 novembre dans le vert, son indice principal, le MASI, s’adjugeant 4,72% à 17.317,91 points (pts). Le MASI.20, qui reflète la performance des cours des 20 entreprises les plus liquides, a gagné 5,57% à 1.264,07 pts, tandis que le MASI ESG, indice des entreprises ayant la meilleure notation ESG selon Moody’s ESG Solutions, a avancé de 7,54% à 1.324,58 pts. Le MASI Mid and Small Cap, qui mesure la performance des petites et moyennes entreprises cotées à la Bourse de Casablanca, a augmenté de 4,28% à 1.623,71 pts. Sur le plan sectoriel, les indices « Participation et promotion immobilières » (+11,5%), « Sociétés de portefeuilles – Holdings » (+9,77%) et « Loisirs et hôtels » (+8,39%) ont signé les meilleures performances. À l’opposé, les secteurs « Chimie » (-1,68%) et « Transport » (-0,12%) ont accusé les uniques baisses. Les échanges ont dépassé 3,46 milliards de dirhams (MMDH), répartis entre le marché de blocs (1,84 MMDH), le marché central (1,6 MMDH) et les transferts (11,68 millions de dirhams), et dominés par les transactions sur Managem (16,18%), Cash Plus (9,54%) et Jet Contractors (9,15%). La capitalisation boursière a, quant à elle, atteint plus de 1.015,93 MMDH. Aux valeurs individuelles, Douja Prom Addoha (+13,49% à 38,7 DH), Résidences Dar Saada (+10,63% à 177 DH), Delta Holding (+9,78% à 49,4 DH), Alliances (+8,89% à 371,2 DH) et Zellidja (+8,67% à 249,95 DH) ont réalisé les meilleures performances. À l’inverse, Maroc Leasing (-5,97% à 338,5 DH), Eqdom (-5,93% à 1.364 DH), Oulmès (-5,52% à 1.130 DH), Involys (-4,31% à 110 DH) et Réalisations Mécaniques (-2% à 440 DH) ont accusé les plus fortes baisses. The post Belle semaine pour la Bourse de Casablanca appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Cenpower celebrates its journey and contribution to Ghana’s energy sector
items.description: Cenpower Generation Ltd (Cenpower), owner of the 350 MW Kpone Independent Power Plant (KIPP), has marked a significant milestone in its development journey by celebrating the decade since the power plant’s sod-cutting ceremony. Held under the theme, “Powering Ghana’s Future Through Reliable and Sustainable Power Generation,” the celebration provided an opportunity to reflect on Cenpower’s journey from a Ghanaian entrepreneurial vision to the successful development and operation of one of Ghana’s major independent power generation facilities, while recognising its contribution to the country’s energy sector. The event brought together government representatives, shareholders, project financiers, and other energy sector stakeholders. Among those present were Her Excellency Professor Jane Naana Opoku-Agyemang, Vice President of the Republic of Ghana, and other distinguished dignitaries. Cenpower’s journey began in 2003 when four Ghanaian entrepreneurs – Samuel Nana Brew-Butler, Dr Jimmy Heymann, Michael Wilson and Kweku Awotwi – incorporated the company to help meet Ghana’s growing demand for electricity. To develop KIPP, Cenpower brought together Ghanaian entrepreneurship, international investment, and technical expertise to deliver the power project. The project achieved financial close in December 2014, followed by the sod-cutting ceremony on 29 January 2015. KIPP subsequently commenced commercial operations on 10 June 2019. Today, the 350 MW combined-cycle gas turbine plant supplies electricity to Ghana’s national grid and contributes to the country’s generation capacity. Since commencing commercial operations, the plant has supplied electricity equivalent to the needs of approximately one million households, reinforcing its role in supporting Ghana’s electricity supply and economic activity. Speaking at the celebration, Prof Jane Naana Opoku-Agyemang, Vice President of the Republic of Ghana, described Cenpower as an example of Ghanaian enterprise and the importance of private-sector participation in developing critical national infrastructure. She noted that projects of this scale demonstrate Ghanaian entrepreneurs’ ability to mobilise investment, build technical expertise, and sustain partnerships to deliver infrastructure that supports national development. The Vice President also highlighted government’s efforts to strengthen Ghana’s energy sector through improved financial management, renegotiated agreements with independent power producers and the promotion of natural gas as a more cost-effective fuel for electricity generation. She commended Cenpower for extending its contribution beyond electricity generation to community and environmental initiatives, including efforts to address plastic pollution and educate students on waste management and electricity conservation. Delivering remarks on behalf of the Minister for Energy and Green Transition, Dr John Abdulai Jinapor, the Ministry’s Director of Power, Suleman Abubakari, commended Cenpower for its contribution to Ghana’s energy security and described KIPP as an important example of what sustained public-private partnerships can achieve. He acknowledged the financial and operational challenges affecting independent power producers and highlighted the Government’s efforts to restore financial discipline, strengthen investor confidence, and improve the electricity sector’s financial sustainability. He also noted that government’s wider energy strategy includes increasing generation capacity, securing additional natural gas supplies, reducing dependence on expensive liquid fuels and modernising transmission and distribution infrastructure. “Our objective is clear: a reliable, affordable and financially sustainable electricity system capable of powering businesses, industrialisation and economic transformation,” he stated. The celebration also highlighted significant developments in Cenpower’s relationship with Government, particularly the renegotiation of its Power Purchase Agreement (PPA). In July 2026, Government approved the Amended and Restated Power Purchase Agreement and related agreements, intended to deliver greater value for Ghanaians while strengthening investor confidence. Parliament also approved the refinancing of Independent Power Producers’ obligations, including those of Cenpower, on 28 July 2026, supporting the project’s long-term financial sustainability. The development was marked by the formal exchange of documents for the Amended and Restated PPA between the Government of Ghana and Cenpower. Under the revised agreement, Cenpower agreed to a US$66 million discount on outstanding arrears owed to the company, which at one point had reached approximately US$400 million. This followed the payment of approximately US$59 million to Cenpower in 2025 as part of government’s efforts to settle legacy debts owed to Independent Power Producers. In addition to the discount, the revised agreement extends Cenpower’s existing PPA by 10 years and reduces the tariff charged by the company. These arrangements are expected to support the plant’s continued operations while contributing to efforts to improve the financial sustainability of Ghana’s power sector and strengthen the partnership between Government and Cenpower. Speaking on the agreement, Samuel Nana Brew-Butler, Chairman of Cenpower Generation Ltd, described the US$66 million discount as a sacrifice the company was willing to make in support of Ghana’s broader energy sector objectives. “So we are able to do the exchange of this document, which is the amended and restated Power Purchase Agreement, which allows us to give a whopping discount to all of you here. So, $66 million. If you remember, I said at one stage, what was outstanding was about $400 million, but it’s our country, so that sacrifice had to be made,” he said. He also acknowledged the 10-year extension granted by the government and the tariff reduction under the revised agreement, describing the development as an important step toward a more sustainable future for the partnership. Mr Samuel Nana Brew-Butler also reflected on the challenges the company faced in developing the project, acknowledging the financial uncertainty and difficult negotiations that marked parts of its journey. He said the company’s determination to find a sustainable solution, supported by continued engagement, constructive negotiations, and its partners’ commitment, helped it reach this important milestone. “It was a hard road to travel, but we did not turn back. We persevered, we kept faith, and today, we have reached an important milestone,” he said. Looking ahead, Mr. Brew-Butler outlined Cenpower’s plans to expand its investments into renewable energy. These include developing 3 MW to 5 MW of rooftop and car park solar capacity at the Kpone facility, as well as a 100 MW solar photovoltaic and battery energy storage project in the Savannah Region, with construction of the first 50 MW phase expected to begin in 2027. He said the investments would support the company’s transition to cleaner energy, improve operational sustainability, and complement conventional power generation in Ghana’s energy mix. Cenpower’s contribution to the energy sector has also been recognised internationally for its operational performance, including recognition under the Operational Reliability Analysis Program (ORAP). This reflects the company’s focus on maintaining reliable plant operations and operational standards within the power generation industry. Beyond electricity generation, Cenpower continues to support the development and wellbeing of its host community through employment opportunities, scholarship support, infrastructure development, and environmental initiatives. At the celebration, Cenpower handed over 100 solar-powered streetlights to the Kpone community as part of its community initiatives, with support from its shareholders. The initiative is intended to improve public lighting and support community safety. Theo Sackey, Chief Executive Officer of Cenpower Generation Ltd, welcomed the Vice President, government representatives, traditional authorities, shareholders, partners and other stakeholders. He acknowledged the support and commitment of the individuals and institutions that contributed to the company’s journey, including those unable to attend the celebration. The programme included reflections from Cenpower’s leadership and project partners, the exchange of documents for the amended PPA, the unveiling of a commemorative plaque and a ribbon-cutting ceremony. As Cenpower reflects on its journey, the company remains focused on its vision of becoming Africa’s best Independent Power Producer while continuing to support Ghana’s energy needs through reliable power generation and sustainable operations.

items.title: CJ shows displeasure over cops making TikTok videos
items.description: LAHORE: Lahore High Court Chief Justice Aalia Neelum on Thursday expressed her displeasure over police officers making TikTok videos about missing girls and uploading them on social media. “How police officers engaged in such activities [making video clips] would trace the missing girls,” the chief justice questioned, hearing a petition filed by a woman, Salma Bibi, seeking recovery of her allegedly missing daughter. The chief justice also expressed dissatisfaction with the committee formed to recover the missing girls and summoned Inspector General of Police (IGP) Abdul Karim in person on Nov 11. Earlier, police officials, including Punjab DIG (Crimes) Ali Janbaz and DIG (Legal) Awais Malik, appeared before the court. A law officer submitted a report on cases involving the abduction and recovery of girls. He said the police recovered 2,810 girls, while 452 remained missing, adding that four of the outstanding cases dated back to 2021. “Where would police look for the cases registered in 2021? We are now in 2026. We cannot wait until 2032 to examine cases registered in 2024,” Chief Justice Neelum observed. The police officers told the court that a social media application had helped trace a considerable number of missing girls. An officer of the investigation wing stated that most of the outstanding cases were reported from Rawalpindi, Sialkot and Nankana Sahib. The chief justice was informed that action would be taken against the police officials involved in making and uploading TikTok videos. She adjourned further proceedings till Nov 11. Published in Dawn, November 6th, 2026

items.title: Melania Trump hosts Russia-Ukraine meeting, calls for ‘enduring’ truce
items.description: WASHINGTON: US First Lady Melania Trump called for a “more enduring” ceasefire in Ukraine as she hosted a rare meeting between officials from the war-torn country and its invader Russia at the White House on Thursday. The unprecedented meeting hoped to build on a localised six-day truce in the starvation-hit Ukrainian city of Oleshky that US President Donald Trump’s wife had announced last month. “Now we must use the courage we brought to Oleshky to find common ground through a shared concern for the suffering of innocent people,” Melania Trump told reporters. “Together, we can create something more enduring than a temporary ceasefire.” The Slovenian-born former model said she was sending the envoys back with personal letters to Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. She urged them to use the Oleshky ceasefire — the longest truce so far in the Russian invasion that began in February 2022 — as a “spark in a world of darkness.” “The ceasefire in Oleshky would not be possible without President Putin and President Zelensky. Their cooperation establishes a meaningful precedent for advancing peace throughout the region,” she added. The rare halt in fighting, which was respected by both sides, allowed roads to be demined and residents to depart for either Ukraine or Russia. Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev said he thanked Melania Trump on Put­in’s behalf for her “distinguished humanitarian role” in brokering the truce in Oleshky and for work on reuniting children separated from their families by the war. They include children allegedly abducted by Russia. Behind-the-scenes diplomacy The White House meeting also reunited Russia’s human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova and her counterpart from Kyiv, Dmytro Lubinets, who formed an unlikely bond during the Oleshky ceasefire. The pair were on the ground in the devastated town, addressing the media together on efforts to evacuate residents and deliver aid, in one of the most substantial instances of cooperation between the warring countries. The US first lady’s efforts come ahead of trilateral talks next week in Abu Dhabi aimed at ending the Ukraine war — the first between Russia, Ukraine and the United States since February. The talks have revived hopes for ending the grinding war, although a recent rapprochement between Donald Trump and Putin has raised concerns the United States could turn its back on Kyiv. Trump had promised to end the Ukraine war within 24 hours of taking office in January 2025 but his peace efforts have been intermittent, with the Iran war taking much of his attention this year. Zelensky said he had a “very detailed, hour-and-a-half-long” conversation with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner ahead of the Abu Dhabi talks. The Ukrainian president awarded Melania Trump a national honour for her role in brokering the Oleshky ceasefire, which Lubinets personally presented at the White House. “I hereby decree that the Order of Princess Olga, First Class, be awarded to Melania Trump, First Lady of the United States of America,” a decree read on the Ukrainian presidential website. The US first lady stunned the world when she announced in October 2025 that she had established a secret channel of communication with Putin in a bid to reunite war-separated children. She has since played a growing but still behind-the-scenes diplomatic role in the Ukraine conflict — even as her husband campaigns openly to win the Nobel Peace Prize despite his own failed efforts to end the war. Published in Dawn, November 6th, 2026

items.title: GUTA urges authorities to act over Chinese malls’ impact on local businesses
items.description: The President of the Ghana Union of Traders’ Associations (GUTA), Clement Boateng, has urged authorities to examine the expansion of Chinese shopping malls, warning that local businesses are losing market share. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express Business Edition on Thursday, he claimed the malls were taking about 60 per cent of local traders’ market share. He said their growing presence was hurting Ghanaian businesses, even as broader economic conditions improved. “But if you want to talk about shops springing up, it’s mostly these Chinese shopping malls which are even in the market.” Mr Boateng questioned how the expansion of these malls could be reconciled with suggestions that the trading environment was poor. “Well, if the environment is that bad, we would not be to the extent that these Chinese shopping malls are springing up, and these shopping malls are taking about 60% of our market share, and we think it is having a very negative impact as far as local businesses, you know, are concerned.” He also raised concerns about where those businesses’ profits would go. He argued that Chinese malls would repatriate their earnings, while stronger local businesses would keep money in the country. GUTA’s call for intervention came alongside a broadly positive assessment of business conditions. Mr Boateng agreed with Ghana National Chamber of Commerce and Industry CEO Mark Badu-Aboagye that economic indicators were moving in a favourable direction. He said traders should feel the benefits in their operations. “So, to a large extent, it hasn’t been all that bad.” However, he maintained that the expansion of Chinese malls required attention from the authorities because of its impact on local traders.

items.title: Obuasi abuse allegations: Coalition demands national child-protection overhaul
items.description: The National Coalition for Proper Human Sexual Rights and Family Values has called for a comprehensive overhaul of Ghana’s child-protection system, warning that the allegations of sexual abuse at the Obuasi Senior High Technical School (SHTS) expose weaknesses that could leave children vulnerable in schools and other institutions. The coalition is demanding a nationwide audit of safeguarding arrangements in educational institutions, the establishment of a National Sex Offenders Register and stronger mechanisms to hold school authorities and other officials accountable for mishandling abuse complaints. It says the response to the Obuasi allegations must go beyond investigating the individuals implicated and address institutional failures that may allow abuse to occur, go unreported or be concealed. In a statement signed by its Executive Secretary, Moses Foh-Amoaning, the coalition said the case should serve as a turning point in the country’s approach to protecting children. It commended investigative journalist Manasseh Azure Awuni for bringing the allegations involving students of Obuasi SHTS to public attention and called for thorough and impartial investigations, protection for complainants and witnesses, and due process for all persons implicated. The coalition said no institution should place its reputation above the safety of children and that allegations of abuse must be handled without intimidation or victimisation. Nationwide safeguarding audit As part of its proposed reforms, the coalition wants the Ministries of Education and Gender, Children and Social Protection, the Ghana Education Service (GES) and relevant regulatory bodies to commission an independent national audit of child-protection arrangements. The proposed review would examine school reporting systems, staff conduct, professional boundaries, boarding-house supervision, institutional responses to previous complaints and the effectiveness of safeguards against retaliation. It also wants the audit to assess whether students have access to confidential counselling and protection services, as well as appropriate referral channels to social welfare agencies and the police. The findings, it said, should inform a publicly available national reform programme with clear timelines, responsibilities and performance indicators, while protecting the identities of affected children. The coalition is also advocating independent reporting channels in schools, particularly where allegations involve headteachers, administrators or other senior officials. It argued that children should not be required to report abuse through the same authority structures implicated in their complaints. “NO CHILD SHOULD HAVE TO SEEK PERMISSION FROM A POTENTIAL ABUSER TO REPORT ABUSE,” the statement said. It further insisted that suspected criminal offences must be referred promptly to the appropriate law enforcement authorities and that internal disciplinary procedures should not be used as substitutes for criminal investigations. Sex offenders register proposed A major part of the coalition’s demands is the establishment of a legally backed National Sex Offenders Register, supported by mandatory safeguarding background checks for people seeking employment in positions involving children. The proposed system would cover teachers, school administrators, boarding staff, caregivers, coaches, youth workers and relevant religious personnel in both public and private institutions. The coalition wants legislation to define the offences that would qualify for registration, the agencies responsible for maintaining the database, access arrangements, retention periods and safeguards for correcting or reviewing information. It also proposes a separate professional barring mechanism to prevent individuals found unsuitable for specified child-facing positions through fair legal proceedings from continuing in such roles. The statement, however, stresses the need to distinguish between criminal convictions, established professional misconduct and unresolved allegations, with appropriate rights of appeal and review. It says the register must serve as a child-protection tool rather than encourage vigilantism or undermine the rights of individuals. The coalition has asked the Attorney-General and Minister for Justice to lead a review of existing criminal and child-protection laws to identify gaps and initiate the necessary legislative changes. Officials must answer for cover-ups The group is also seeking investigations and sanctions against officials who deliberately obstruct inquiries, intimidate witnesses, destroy evidence or suppress reports of abuse. It wants a national child-safeguarding accountability framework under which relevant institutions periodically publish anonymised information on complaints received, investigations completed, disciplinary outcomes, criminal referrals and support services provided to affected children. The proposed framework, it said, should make the performance of institutions measurable without exposing the identities or private information of children. The coalition further wants child-safeguarding compliance to become a mandatory part of school inspections and leadership assessments by the National Schools Inspectorate Authority (NaSIA), GES and other education regulators. Protection must extend beyond schools The coalition said child protection should not be confined to educational institutions but must also be strengthened in homes, religious bodies and traditional communities. It has called on the Ministry of Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs to work with religious organisations, traditional authorities and child-protection stakeholders to establish enforceable safeguarding standards and independent complaint mechanisms for religious and cultural institutions. It also wants a national family-strengthening and community child-protection initiative to promote responsible parenting, positive discipline, digital safety, healthy family relationships and early reporting of abuse. The coalition said children must be taught about personal dignity, bodily safety, healthy boundaries and respect for others, while parents and guardians must create environments in which children can disclose abuse without fear of blame. It also stressed that boys who experience sexual abuse must receive the same protection and attention as girls, warning that stigma and cultural attitudes could discourage male survivors from reporting assaults. Stakeholder meeting planned As part of its proposed action plan, the coalition said it had initiated arrangements for a national stakeholder consultation within two weeks of its October 30 statement. The proposed meeting is expected to bring together government ministries and agencies, the Attorney-General’s Department, the Judiciary and Judicial Service, the police, education authorities, child-protection organisations, civil society groups and professional bodies. The engagement is intended to examine practical ways of implementing the proposed reforms and agree on priority actions, institutional responsibilities, timelines and accountability measures. The coalition said it was prepared to work with the relevant institutions to expand its existing safeguarding training engagements with the GES and strengthen the capacity of education personnel to recognise, prevent and respond to abuse involving children. It maintained that the Obuasi SHTS allegations should lead to lasting institutional changes rather than another round of public outrage followed by inaction. “LET OBUASI SHTS BE MORE THAN A SCANDAL,” the statement said. items.title: Goods delayed, banks demanding repayment – GUTA President details traders’ pressures
items.description: Rising cargo volumes are causing port congestion and delaying goods clearance, the President of the Ghana Union of Traders’ Associations (GUTA), Clement Boateng, said. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express Business Edition on Thursday, he identified clearance delays as one of the pressures facing traders, alongside longer shipping times from the United Arab Emirates. “As far as clearance is concerned, at the port, because of the huge volumes of cargo that is coming now, it has also resulted in some delays.” Mr Boateng said business conditions in 2026 were generally not bad. But disruptions to shipments from the UAE were affecting traders. He attributed the shipping difficulties to the war and developments at the Strait of Hormuz. He said these forced vessels to reroute and extended delivery times. Goods expected within 45 to 60 days were now taking about three to four months to arrive. Traders then had to clear them at the port, where congestion added to delays. The longer wait is also pressuring traders who finance their imports with bank loans. Mr Boateng said repayments begin the month after a facility is taken, leaving borrowers facing demands while their goods are still in transit. “And assuming you’ve gone to take a facility from the bank, they will be on your neck because once you take a facility from them, the repayment starts the following month.” He renewed his call for banks to grant borrowers a moratorium before repayments begin. This would give traders breathing space as they wait for shipments to arrive and clear their goods. His account highlights two sources of delay for importers: extended shipping journeys and congestion during clearance. For those relying on borrowed funds, the repayment schedule adds further pressure before the goods become available for sale.

items.title: Choose engineering over business degrees – Salem Kalmoni advises youth
items.description: Young Ghanaians have been encouraged to pursue engineering and other technical disciplines rather than follow the growing preference for business administration qualifications, which are increasingly common in the job market. The Group Chief Executive Officer of Japan Motors Network, Salem Kalmoni, believes specialised technical skills offer young people a stronger foundation for professional growth and leadership, particularly in industries that require practical knowledge and problem-solving abilities. He said he would make a different academic choice if given another opportunity, opting for industrial engineering instead of business administration. Speaking on Joy FM’s Personality Profile with Lexis Bill on Thursday, November 5, Mr Kalmoni said his initial decision to study business administration was largely influenced by the expectation that he would eventually take charge of the family enterprise. “My father had drilled into me that you will take over. You’re the crown prince, and it’s about business. Take over the business, so I had it in my mind that I should take business administration,” he said. However, reflecting on his career and the demands of running a large enterprise, he said industrial engineering would have equipped him with a broader range of practical competencies. “If I were to do it again, I would have taken industrial engineering,” he said, explaining that the discipline would have provided useful knowledge in factory operations, supply chain management and project management. Mr Kalmoni said such technical expertise could later be complemented with business education and management experience. ‘Technical skills matter’ He expressed concern about what he considers an excessive preference among young people for business-related qualifications, arguing that the growing number of graduates in the field has reduced their distinctiveness in the employment market. “I see too many people taking business. Actually, more and more, imagine I have an MBA person in my company, having an MBA who is a cashier now. Business degrees have become commoditised. I think they’ve lost value,” he said. He urged students to consider disciplines such as engineering, which provide specialised skills that can be applied across different sectors of the economy. According to him, people with engineering backgrounds can subsequently acquire management qualifications and move into leadership positions, but the reverse transition from a business background into engineering is often more difficult. “A lot of engineers actually eventually end up with a business degree. You can easily do that. I know many engineers who have become, who have later gone into management and an MBA,” he said. He added: “I don’t know of any business person or social studies person who has become an engineer.” Mr Kalmoni said young people should therefore place greater emphasis on acquiring practical and technical competencies before adding business management qualifications to their education. “I would encourage the youth to take technical courses and engineering degrees. The business is always there. You can always take it and experience it,” he said. From business graduate to industry leader Mr Kalmoni’s reflections draw on his own experience leading a major family-owned automotive enterprise. He studied for a Bachelor of Business Administration in Canada, completing the programme in 1988, before joining Japan Motors in 1991. He later obtained an Executive Master’s degree in Governance and Leadership from the Ghana Institute of Management and Public Administration and completed an Advanced Management Programme at Harvard Business School in 2012. He is a third-generation member of the Kalmoni family, whose business interests grew from a transport and trading enterprise established by his grandfather, Salem Kalmoni, in 1920. Japan Motors Trading Company emerged from the family business in 1962 and was incorporated as a limited liability company in 1965. The company became a major distributor of Japanese vehicles and expanded into vehicle assembly, equipment and other automotive-related operations. Mr Kalmoni led Japan Motors Ghana as Managing Director before his elevation to Group Chief Executive Officer of Japan Motors Network in 2026, with the network operating across several West African markets. His recommendation to young people is that professional preparation should go beyond obtaining management qualifications, with technical knowledge and industry-specific skills providing a valuable foundation for future leadership.

items.title: GUTA President calls for loan repayment moratorium as shipment delays hit traders
items.description: The Ghana Union of Traders Association (GUTA) President Clement Boateng has called for a moratorium on loan repayments to give traders breathing space as shipment delays leave them facing bank demands before their goods arrive. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express Business Edition on Thursday, he said shipments from the United Arab Emirates were taking about three to four months to reach Ghana. Previously, goods were expected within 45 to 60 days. He attributed the longer journey to rerouting linked to the war and developments at the Strait of Hormuz. The delays, he said, put pressure on traders who borrow to finance imports. Loan repayments begin the month after they take the facility, even when their goods are still in transit. “And assuming you’ve gone to take a facility from the bank, they will be on your neck because once you take a facility from them, it the repayment starts the following month.” Mr Boateng said he had repeatedly called for a grace period on repayments. He wants lenders to give traders more time before requiring them to begin servicing their loans. “When we take a facility, the repayment shouldn’t start after just one month.” His appeal centres on the gap between borrowing to buy goods and receiving them for clearance. With shipments taking longer, traders face repayment obligations while waiting for their imports. Arrival at the port does not necessarily end the wait. Mr Boateng said congestion was also slowing clearance, adding another layer of delays for businesses. “because of the huge volumes of cargo that is coming now, it has also resulted in some delays.” Despite these difficulties, he said the broader business environment in 2026 had not been entirely negative. “if you want to talk about the generality of business in 2026, it is not all that bad.” His concern, however, was the pressure on importers caught between longer shipping times, port congestion and loan repayments that start before their goods arrive.

items.title: Telecel Ghana Foundation expands Homecoming to support over 500 patients nationwide
items.description: The Telecel Ghana Foundation has launched the 2026 edition of its annual flagship Homecoming initiative, aiming to discharge over 500 insolvent patients across 16 government health facilities nationwide. Launched at the Shai Osudoku District Hospital in Dodowa, the Foundation settled the outstanding medical bills of 29 patients who had completed treatment but could not return home because they could not afford them. The Foundation also provided NHIS registration and renewal for 120 people, strengthening their sustainable access to healthcare beyond immediate intervention. Rita Agyeiwaa Rockson, Head of Foundation, Sustainability and External Communications at Telecel Ghana, said the initiative was established to ensure that financial hardship does not prevent recovered patients from returning to their families. “No patient should remain in hospital simply because they are unable to pay their medical bills. Unfortunately, this reality continues to affect many families across Ghana, which is why the Telecel Foundation established the Homecoming initiative. “Through Homecoming, we work with selected government hospitals and the Department of Social Welfare to identify and support patients who are medically fit for discharge but cannot return home because of outstanding bills. “This year, we aim to discharge over 500 patients across 16 government health facilities nationwide. For us, recovery should always lead home,” she said. The 2026 edition is the Foundation’s most extensive Homecoming intervention to date. Since its inception in 2011, the initiative has provided relief to financially vulnerable patients while helping participating hospitals recover outstanding bills and make beds available to other patients requiring care. Beyond supporting patients, the Foundation presented essential maternal-health equipment to the Shai Osudoku District Hospital to support healthcare professionals and improve service delivery. Dr Alexander Adjei, Medical Director of the Shai Osudoku District Hospital, welcomed the intervention and described it as an example of how partnerships can improve healthcare outcomes. “Healthcare delivery thrives on strong partnerships. At the hospital level, limited resources and financial constraints can affect our ability to respond to growing patient needs, making collaborations like this extremely important. “We are grateful to the Telecel Ghana Foundation for supporting patients through the Homecoming initiative and for providing essential equipment to strengthen healthcare delivery at our facility. “Through partnerships like this, we can continue to improve our services and share more positive stories from Ghana’s healthcare sector,” Dr Adjei said. For Florence, one of the beneficiaries, the intervention ended more than two weeks of uncertainty after she completed her treatment but could not settle her hospital bill. “All I wanted was to return home, but my family and I did not have the money to pay the bill. As a pregnant woman, I wanted to be with my family, where I could rest, eat well, and take better care of myself and my baby. “When I heard that the Telecel Ghana Foundation had settled my bill, I felt a heavy burden lift off me. I can finally go home and focus on having a healthy pregnancy. I am truly grateful for this support,” Florence said. The launch marked the beginning of a nationwide rollout across the Southern, Northern and Middle belts from 4 November to 7 December 2026. Following the intervention at the Shai Osudoku District Hospital, the Southern Belt phase will continue at Anfoega Hospital, Eastern Regional Hospital, Cape Coast Teaching Hospital and Kwesimintsim Hospital. The initiative will subsequently move to selected facilities in the Northern and Middle belts. The 2026 Homecoming initiative is being implemented in partnership with the Ghana Health Service, participating government health facilities and The Medical Reformist. Through the expanded initiative, the Telecel Ghana Foundation continues its commitment to helping recovered patients return home with dignity, easing the burden on vulnerable families and strengthening healthcare delivery across Ghana.

items.title: Rule of the people?
items.description: THE resounding defeat of the Republican Party in the US midterm election this week has triggered celebratory chatter around the world. Many see it as the beginning of the end for Donald Trump; the vibe was very similar when Trump was defeated by Joe Biden in the 2020 US presidential election. Yet four years later, Trumpism proved to be alive and very well. Trump cannot stand in the 2028 presidential election. For that reason alone, his political career is reaching its end. But that does not mean that Trumpism — both the ideology and the social base to which it speaks — will disappear alongside the man himself. Here I offer some suggestions what this latest election signals about the future of democracy in the US, and, by extension, around the world. We should harbour no illusions about the power of big money in American politics, or the Democratic Party’s historical commitment to US empire — the Biden administration’s diabolical warmongering after Oct 7, 2023, in Gaza, after all, set the stage for Trump’s 2024 win. Given this backdrop, the victory of candidates like Abdul el-Sayed who oppose imperialist wars abroad and are fronting progressive economic policies at home — just like Zohran Mamdani did during his successful campaign to become New York mayor — confirms that societal attitudes are changing. A growing number of young Americans now view socialism favourably and want unconditional support for Israel to be discontinued. It is another matter entirely whether an increasingly influential left-wing of the Democratic Party can win the inner-party struggle and then the presidency. The contemporary state is whittling away democratic freedoms. While progressive ideology has gained a foothold in American society, the Trumpist right maintains its powerful, and mobilised MAGA base , sustained in part by Christian evangelicals. Before his win in 2024, Trump vowed to stop fighting wars abroad, and bring back industrial jobs and prosperity. His base has been antagonised by the disastrous and prolonged war on Iran, and the inflationary spiral it has triggered. Vice-President J.D. Vance has already acknowledged this , and even added that Washington’s ‘special relationship’ with Israel must change. Trumpism will not die out because of a midterm defeat. Long-term economic stagnation will give it social mooring, while its major ideological enemies — immigration, the left, and outsourcing — remain easy sells. A useful analogy is that of Brazil, where Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva recently staved off the most recent articulation of Bolsanarismo — the parallel ideology to Trumpism — to win his fourth term as president. Brazil’s left has far greater social roots than the emergent Democratic left in the US, hence its ability to mobilise the last-minute votes necessary to re-elect Lula. But the far right under the leadership of the Bolsanaro family also has a mobilised social base, which will rebound from the election loss. Lula is 81, and his Workers Party will have to deepen the social struggle to keep Bolsanarismo at bay in the years to come. Zooming out further, the right wing is ascendant across much of the world, while the contemporary state is whittling away democratic freedoms and paving the way for capital to carry on with business as usual. Electoral victories for left-of-centre candidates in the US, Brazil or wherever else they may come to pass will not produce structural change in isolation. Does going to the ballot allow ordinary people an opportunity to exercise political choice? Yes. But this is not the same as working-class majorities being organised for progressive social transformation. The latter is re­­quired both to ensure more significant electo­r­­al success and then to turn such victories into su­­bstantive cha­­­nge. Of course, we in Pakistan do not even get to enjoy the unfettered right to vote. The military-bureaucratic oligarchy that has ruled over us from soon after 1947 did not even allow a general election until 1970, and then chose military action rather than handing over power to the winning party afterwards. More recently, the electoral mandate in the 2024 general election was stolen blatantly, culminating in the imposition of emergency in KP . There is something to be said for at least the temporary waves of hope that are generated by electoral victories, even if one should at the same time be conscious of the highly delimited nature of democracy under the rule of contemporary capital. Progressives in Pakistan have to fight an epic battle against tyranny to even retain the pretence that democracy means rule of the people. And then we have to come up with a shared project for how to run a country ravaged by violence, repression and a deep crisis of identity. The writer teaches at Quaid-i-Azam University, Islamabad. Published in Dawn, November 6th, 2026

items.title: Morocco’s King Mohammed VI orders coordination of MINURSO withdrawal, reaffirms ceasefire commitment
items.description: Morocco’s King Mohammed VI has directed the government to coordinate and support the withdrawal of the United Nations mission in Western Sahara, while reaffirming the kingdom’s commitment to the ceasefire. The instructions followed a working session at the Royal Palace in Rabat on November 4, 2026, according to a Royal Office statement. The meeting addressed the next steps after the UN Security Council did not renew MINURSO’s mandate on October 30. The UN has confirmed that the mission has ceased operations and entered a liquidation period. King Mohammed VI instructed the Interior Ministry’s Office for Coordination with MINURSO to assist with the mission’s withdrawal. The Royal Office said the aim was to ensure a smooth and orderly process in cooperation with the United Nations. The King also reaffirmed Morocco’s commitment to the ceasefire, saying the end of the mission’s mandate would not alter that position. During the session, he emphasised Morocco’s territorial integrity, national security and the safety of residents in the territory, which the kingdom refers to as its Southern Provinces. He directed the officials responsible to implement these priorities firmly and vigilantly, while maintaining development programmes and major infrastructure projects. Head of Government Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri, royal adviser Fouad Ali El Himma, and Interior Minister Abdelouafi Laftit attended the meeting. Lieutenant General Mohammed Berrid, Inspector General of the Royal Armed Forces and Commander of the South Zone, also participated. According to the Royal Office, officials were instructed to monitor developments and maintain the kingdom’s previously stated position on the dispute. The statement reiterated Morocco’s commitment to its international obligations and to pursuing peace while safeguarding its sovereignty. It also restated the kingdom’s position that autonomy offers the political solution to the conflict, citing support from countries that recognise Morocco’s sovereignty over Western Sahara.

items.title: Raise your children to carry the business torch — Salem Kalmoni advises Ghanaian entrepreneurs
items.description: Ghanaian entrepreneurs have been urged to introduce their children to their businesses from an early age to prepare them for leadership and improve the chances of enterprises surviving beyond their founders. The Chief Executive Officer of Japan Motors Ghana, Salem Kalmoni, says exposing children to the daily operations of a family business while they are young helps them understand its values, culture and responsibilities long before they are expected to take over. He said the approach had been central to his own upbringing, recalling how his father involved him in business activities when he was a child because he was the firstborn. Speaking on Joy FM’s Personality Profile with Lexis Bill on Thursday, November 5, Mr Kalmoni said his father regularly took him to social events he attended and introduced him to different aspects of the family’s business during school holidays. “One thing about family businesses is that you involve your children, especially the firstborn. I was the firstborn,” he said. “And perhaps this is one lesson for aspiring multi-generational Ghanaian family businesses: involve your children in the business from youth. From a very early age. Get them in.” He also recalled accompanying his father to the family’s farm on the outskirts of Accra, which later became the Lakeside Estate development. The farm, he said, was known as Agricattle in the early 1970s, and those visits formed part of his early exposure to the family’s business interests. Mr Kalmoni said the experience offered an important lesson for Ghanaian entrepreneurs seeking to build enterprises that could be sustained by successive generations. A challenge for family businesses His advice comes against the background of concerns about the ability of family-owned enterprises in Ghana to survive changes in ownership and leadership. Although such businesses contribute to employment, investment and economic activity, succession remains a major challenge. A PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) report published in 2014 indicated that about 43 per cent of family businesses did not have succession plans, while only approximately 12 per cent survived to the third generation. The figures underline the importance of preparing potential successors before the founder or current leadership exits the business. Research into family-owned enterprises in Ghana has also identified succession as a gradual process requiring preparation, training and the support of other family members and stakeholders. A family business legacy Mr Kalmoni’s experience reflects the generational transition he is encouraging other business owners to pursue. Japan Motors Trading Company Limited traces its roots to Kalmoni & Sons, a family trading and transport business established by his grandfather, the late Salem Kalmoni, in 1920. The family business expanded into motor vehicle distribution after importing a Datsun, now Nissan, vehicle into Ghana in 1958. Japan Motors Trading Company emerged from the enterprise in 1962 and was incorporated as a limited liability company in 1965. The company has since developed into a major player in Ghana’s automotive industry, representing international vehicle and equipment brands and expanding its operations beyond Ghana. Mr Kalmoni, a third-generation member of the family, joined the company in 1991 after completing his studies in Canada and has led its operations, overseeing its expansion in Ghana and other West African markets.

items.title: A bleak economic future
items.description: ROBERT Lucas, a towering figure of 20th-century macroeconomics and a Nobel laureate, opined on economic growth and the standard of living that “the consequences for human welfare involved in questions like these are simply staggering: once one starts to think about them, it is hard to think about anything else” (On the Mechanics of Economic Development, 1988). The context of his observation was the significant differences in standards of living across the globe. I contemplated the same — specifically, whether our economic future might offer us some respite from our perennial failures. Sadly, it does not look good. What follows is a brief narration of various considerations that led me to this conclusion. The incentives and structure of the economy resemble anything but a viable plan for sustained improvement in living standards and chances of shared prosperity. Tellingly, Pakistan now has the unique distinction of being the only country in the world where three different arrangements compete for a limited set of resources. The first is the formal sector, which mainly comprises an extremely unproductive and extractive public sector. The second is the ‘deep state’, growing within the bosom of the public sector (formally and informally) and meeting its growing economic interests through forced ingress. The third is the ‘informal’ sector, estimated at about 35 to 40 per cent of the formal economy, that tries its best to stay away from formality. The implications of continuing this arrangement now and in the future are not well understood. There is little, if any, chance, for example, of an entrepreneur arising who could upend traditional industries and usher in economies of scale or creative disruption. It follows, then, that we will remain stuck with low-productivity, rentier industries like sugar that rely on legislative rents (taxpayer-financed subsidies) and tariff protection to shield them from competition. The incentives and structure of the economy resemble anything but a viable plan for sustained improvement in living standards. An even more damning predicament is the continuation of economic management as merely an accounting exercise to balance the books. From having some of the worst development indicators to the absurdity of taking foreign loans for purposes such as pension reforms, the adverse spillovers of this mediocrity are well known. Yet one is astonished to see such pedestrian management celebrated officially. Witness the bewildering displays of vainglorious puffery under the banner of ‘nationalism’. At the same time, trade with three of our neighbours is almost non-existent, a situation akin to a contraction of the available resource envelope and growth possibilities. This attitude helps explain why we, the world’s fifth most populous country, account for less than 1pc of the massive $35 trillion global trade in goods and services. What we have done to our human capital is another indicator of our dim prospects. Since at least the time of Adam Smith’s seminal work (1776), it has been understood that it is the most valuable input in the process of economic growth, something that Paul Romer’s endogenous growth theory (1990) put an authoritative stamp upon. Developing this input has always remained low on our priorities. An even more grievous spectre now haunts our economy: the flight of quality human capital. It is officially celebrated as an achievement in the context of remittances. Still, no policymaker is willing to realise that the full value of quality human capital is captured outside Pakistan. Think of the innumerable examples of people who have made a name for themselves abroad. What if they had remained here and invested their time, resources, and effort to create wealth at home? Or are we just happy to receive a pittance of that effort in the form of remittances that merely sustain consumption? The ‘Lucas critique’ of the 1970s, which transformed macroeconomics, implies that people respond to policy regimes by revising their expectations. The steady flight of skilled people from Pakistan, a trend since the 1970s, has accelerated sharply in recent decades, suggesting that citizens’ expectations of the country’s future have turned deeply pessimistic. This is reflected in what young people think. Having taught at several universities, I can attest that the majority of students view their education as a stepping stone to settling abroad. For those who cannot make it to foreign shores and are active in the workforce, a difficult predicament under a poorly designed incentive structure awaits. Try justifying, logically, how in a country with one of the lowest labour force participation rates, the salaried class gets bilked for more than Rs2tr of its income in the last five years, while record inflation has decimated purchasing power for the majority. The obvious lesson (which then spills over into expectations) is that the main beneficiary of workers’ effort is the government’s coffers rather than the person. Better then to try one’s luck elsewhere. This hollowing out, which will continue, leaves the public sector and its PSDPs as the major avenue of growth. This system spawns corruption, multi-trillion liabilities, and waste (the burden of which ultimately falls upon the taxpayer). Lahore is the most pertinent example among Pakistani cities, with the second-largest economy and one of the highest per capita incomes. Yet it regularly tops the world’s most polluted city rankings rather than quality-of-life rankings, thanks mainly to brick-and-mortar-based PSDPs. Any material gains are more than offset by deteriorating air quality and rising health costs. I can continue in this manner — for instance, by pointing out that the legislature is held hostage by the same people who have been there for at least three decades, with no meaningful economic reform emerging during their tenure. It is further compromised by their progeny, who inhabit both Houses. But I am sure the reader gets the gist of my argument: the chances that we will witness a significant turnaround in our economic fortunes are remote. We will likely remain saddled with a state whose main aim, as Marx described it, is ‘nothing else’ other than extracting taxes. At least that’s how I see it. Bob Lucas, I posit, would also have nodded in approval. The writer is an economist. His current research focuses on the long-term analysis of various issues plaguing Pakistan’s economy, as well as economic reforms and the history of economic thought. X: @ShahidMohmand79 shahid.mohmand@gmail.com Published in Dawn, November 6th, 2026

items.title: Produits de santé : L’AMMPS lance deux plateformes numériques pour signaler les effets indésirables
items.description: L’Agence marocaine des médicaments et des produits de santé (AMMPS) a annoncé, mercredi 4 novembre, le lancement de deux plateformes numériques destinées à recueillir les signalements d’événements indésirables liés aux médicaments, aux vaccins et à différents produits de santé. L’objectif est de renforcer la surveillance de leur sécurité et de permettre une détection plus précoce des risques potentiels associés à leur utilisation. Présentés comme de nouveaux outils de vigilance sanitaire, VigiMobile et VigiUp s’adressent aussi bien aux citoyens qu’aux professionnels de santé. Dans un communiqué, l’agence détaille les fonctions de ces deux dispositifs, mis à disposition par son Centre national de vigilance sanitaire et de gestion des risques. L’application VigiMobile est consacrée au signalement des événements indésirables liés aux médicaments et aux vaccins. La plateforme VigiUp couvre, quant à elle, un champ plus large de produits de santé, notamment les dispositifs médicaux, les réactifs utilisés dans le diagnostic de laboratoire, les produits d’hygiène corporelle et de cosmétique, ainsi que les compléments alimentaires. Les deux outils se veulent accessibles et simples d’utilisation. Les citoyens et les professionnels de santé peuvent y accéder depuis le site officiel de l’Agence marocaine des médicaments et des produits de santé, à l’adresse www.ammps.gov.ma. Renforcer la vigilance sanitaire Le lancement officiel des plateformes a été marqué par une cérémonie organisée en présence du secrétaire général du ministère de la Santé et de la Protection sociale, de responsables institutionnels, de représentants d’établissements de santé et de professionnels du secteur. L’événement s’inscrit dans le cadre de la campagne internationale de sensibilisation à la sécurité des médicaments, « MedSafetyWeek 2026 », qui se déroule du 2 au 8 novembre sous le slogan : « Événements indésirables : ne les ignorez pas, signalez-les ». Lors de cette cérémonie, le secrétaire général du ministère de la Santé et de la Protection sociale a souligné la nécessité de développer les mécanismes de vigilance sanitaire afin d’accompagner les réformes engagées dans le système national de santé. Il a également appelé à renforcer la culture du signalement et la coordination entre les différents intervenants, aux niveaux national et territorial. Le directeur général de l’AMMPS, le professeur Samir Ahid, a, pour sa part, mis en avant les efforts engagés pour moderniser les dispositifs de contrôle et de suivi. Il a insisté sur l’importance d’améliorer les capacités de détection précoce des risques sanitaires et de faciliter la participation des citoyens et des professionnels de santé à la surveillance des médicaments et des produits de santé. Le responsable a également plaidé pour le renforcement du réseau territorial de vigilance sanitaire, à travers une meilleure coordination entre les différents acteurs du système de santé. Cette démarche doit permettre d’améliorer le suivi et le signalement des événements indésirables associés aux produits de santé. Une campagne de sensibilisation à l’échelle nationale La cérémonie a également donné lieu à une session de discussion consacrée à la place du signalement dans le dispositif de vigilance sanitaire. Les échanges ont notamment porté sur le rôle des professionnels de santé dans l’identification des événements indésirables et sur leur contribution à la prévention des risques et à la sécurité des patients. En parallèle du lancement de VigiMobile et VigiUp , l’agence prévoit un programme de sensibilisation déployé aux niveaux national et régional. Celui-ci comprend des actions dans les établissements universitaires à destination des futurs professionnels de santé, ainsi que des campagnes de terrain organisées en coordination avec le réseau des centres régionaux de vigilance sanitaire. The post Produits de santé : L’AMMPS lance deux plateformes numériques pour signaler les effets indésirables appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Reviewing ties
items.description: ALTHOUGH US President Donald Trump has two more years in the White House, the resounding Democratic victory in Tuesday’s midterm elections, handing both Houses of Congress to the latter party, will have a definite impact on how the American leader deals with both internal issues and foreign relations. For one, the Democrats will step up legislative scrutiny of Mr Trump’s domestic agenda, as well as his dealings with foreign states. It is likely that many countries, including Pakistan, might have to recalibrate their policies accordingly. The Trump administration’s relationship with Pakistan has been quite warm, with the American president frequently praising this country’s civil and military leadership publicly. Pakistan’s leadership has returned the compliment, heaping praise on the US leader at international fora, even nominating him for a Nobel Peace Prize. But with the Democrats clawing back power in Congress, changes in America’s approach to global engagement are likely to occur. Traditionally, the relationship between Pakistan and the Democrats has been complicated, and the country has had an easier time working with the Republicans. For example, bilateral ties during Joe Biden’s administration ranged from lukewarm to ambivalent. Matters changed significantly when Mr Trump returned to the White House in January 2025. Washington’s interest in Pakistan’s crypto and minerals sectors is largely seen as a by-product of the American president’s close ties with the country’s rulers. But as the White House’s internal and external dealings come under greater scrutiny when a Democrat-led Congress starts business in January, Pakistan should be prepared for attitudes to change — and not necessarily for the better. America’s hesitation to entertain Pakistan’s request for a $10bn Exchange Stabilisation Support Facility could be a telling sign in this regard. However, even with the Democrats controlling Congress, Pakistan-US ties do not have to nosedive. While relations over the decades have been largely transactional — fighting communism, terrorism, etc — Pakistan should focus on building institutional relations with the US that can weather the storms in Washington. It is true that warm personal ties with whoever occupies the White House can improve relations to a considerable extent. But Pakistan should work with all tiers of the US government — an association that should be based on mutual respect and benefit. Above all, Pakistan must keep its own interest paramount. Durable ties with the US are important, but they should not come at the expense of Pakistan’s other vital relationships, in particular with China. In fact, in the long term, it is in America’s own interest to adopt a more balanced approach in South Asia for the sake of regional stability. Published in Dawn, November 6th, 2026
